## ********************************Lee Zeldin********************************

* * *

### ********************************Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency********************************

![Image 38: Lee Zeldin](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Lee-Zeldin.jpg)

Lee Zeldin is a former United States Congressman who represented New York’s First Congressional District from 2015 to 2023. In 2022, Zeldin made national headlines by nearly winning New York’s gubernatorial race, garnering the most votes for a Republican candidate statewide since Nelson Rockefeller over 50 years earlier. His strong performance at the top of the ticket helped Republicans flip multiple suburban House districts in New York, resulting in the Republican Party’s majority in the House of Representatives.

Born and raised in Suffolk County, New York, at just 23, Lee Zeldin became the youngest attorney in New York at the time. Zeldin served four years on active duty in the U.S. Army, where he held roles as a Military Intelligence Officer, Prosecutor, and Military Magistrate. In the summer of 2006, Lee Zeldin deployed to Iraq with an infantry battalion of fellow paratroopers from the Army’s elite 82nd Airborne Division in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Today, he continues his service as a Lieutenant Colonel in the U.S. Army Reserve, marking over two decades in the military. In 2010, Zeldin was elected to the New York State Senate, where he served until 2014, when he won a seat in Congress. During his eight years in Congress, Zeldin served on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Financial Services Committee. As one of two Jewish Republicans in Congress, he co-chaired the House Republican Israel Caucus, which had over 100 members. He was a vocal advocate on foreign policy, border security, military affairs, combating antisemitism, environmental issues, energy policy, and much more.

For his district, he championed vast infrastructure and research projects, including the preservation of Plum Island, Army Corps of Engineers initiatives, and a $2 billion Electron-Ion Collider for Brookhaven National Lab.

Lee Zeldin currently resides on Long Island, in New York State, with his wife, Diana. Their twin daughters, Mikayla and Arianna, recently left for college, marking an exciting new chapter for their family.

# President Trump Nominates Tim Thomas to Serve as ARC Federal Co-Chair

*    January 8, 2018  
*   **Media Contact:** 

*   [ARC Updates](https://www.arc.gov/newsroom_topic/arc-updates/)

*   [Federal Update](https://www.arc.gov/newsroom_types/federal-updates/)

On January 4, 2018, President Donald Trump [announced his intent to nominate](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-key-additions-administration-27/) Tim Thomas to serve as the next federal co-chair of the Appalachian Regional Commission. Thomas currently serves on the state staff of U.S. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell as a field representative based in the senator’s Bowling Green office. A native Kentuckian, Thomas previously served in the administration of former Kentucky Governor Ernie Fletcher as a special assistant to the secretary of the Kentucky Environmental Cabinet, handling matters including legislative initiatives for the agency. While at the cabinet, Thomas also served as federal facilities coordinator, overseeing environmental regulation of federal sites including U.S. Department of Energy and United States Army installations. Thomas’ last position in state government was as executive director of the Kentucky Infrastructure Authority, an agency tasked with helping finance the expansion of water and wastewater services throughout the state. After leaving state government, Thomas was employed by Swift & Staley, Inc., a government infrastructure support services contractor based in western Kentucky. He is a graduate of Murray State University and the University of Louisville School of Law.
The nomination was referred to the U.S. Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works on January 8 for consideration and review. Once confirmed by the Senate, Thomas will succeed the current ARC federal co-chair, Earl F. Gohl. Gohl has served as federal co-chair since 2010 under appointment by President Obama.

# President Trump Nominates Tim Thomas to Serve as ARC Federal Co-Chair

*    January 8, 2018  
*   **Media Contact:** 

*   [ARC Updates](https://www.arc.gov/newsroom_topic/arc-updates/)

*   [Federal Update](https://www.arc.gov/newsroom_types/federal-updates/)

On January 4, 2018, President Donald Trump [announced his intent to nominate](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/president-donald-j-trump-announces-key-additions-administration-27/) Tim Thomas to serve as the next federal co-chair of the Appalachian Regional Commission. Thomas currently serves on the state staff of U.S. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell as a field representative based in the senator’s Bowling Green office. A native Kentuckian, Thomas previously served in the administration of former Kentucky Governor Ernie Fletcher as a special assistant to the secretary of the Kentucky Environmental Cabinet, handling matters including legislative initiatives for the agency. While at the cabinet, Thomas also served as federal facilities coordinator, overseeing environmental regulation of federal sites including U.S. Department of Energy and United States Army installations. Thomas’ last position in state government was as executive director of the Kentucky Infrastructure Authority, an agency tasked with helping finance the expansion of water and wastewater services throughout the state. After leaving state government, Thomas was employed by Swift & Staley, Inc., a government infrastructure support services contractor based in western Kentucky. He is a graduate of Murray State University and the University of Louisville School of Law.
The nomination was referred to the U.S. Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works on January 8 for consideration and review. Once confirmed by the Senate, Thomas will succeed the current ARC federal co-chair, Earl F. Gohl. Gohl has served as federal co-chair since 2010 under appointment by President Obama.

# Cockrum, et al. v. Trump for President, Inc.

![Image 1: Keyboard](https://protectdemocracy.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Untitled-design-26.png)Overview
### Overview

Three Americans sued the Trump Campaign for violating their privacy and civil rights.

The plaintiffs are a Reagan-era foreign service officer who grew increasingly worried about the direction of our national politics, a staffer who was making good on a lifelong dream to work in Washington, DC for causes he believed in, and a lottery winner who became a philanthropist to spend his winnings for the greater good.

The complaint alleges that, after Russian hackers stole Democratic National Committee emails, their private information was published to the world as part of a calculated political strategy in which the Trump campaign played a central role. The complaint further alleges that the result was a gross violation of their rights under federal civil rights law, which prohibits conspiracies to injure Americans because of their participation in a presidential election.

No American should fear that the consequence of participating in our democracy is that their identity would be stolen or their personal, private information plastered on the Internet for all to see.

Frequently Asked Questions
### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Didn’t President Trump claim he’d already won this case?**

A:[He did](https://twitter.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1015278594795417600), but as numerous reporters pointed out, he was mistaken. The plaintiffs first filed this case in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia in July 2017. On July 3, 2018, that court dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds, holding that the District of Columbia was “the wrong forum for plaintiffs’ lawsuit.” The Judge went out of her way in issuing that ruling to state: “it bears emphasizing that this Court’s ruling is not based on a finding that there was no collusion between defendants and Russia during the 2016 presidential election.” Protect Democracy disagreed with that ruling, but has now filed the case in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, where the Trump Campaign is incorporated and where therefore the court unquestionably has jurisdiction.

**Q. If some of the leaked information was newsworthy, doesn’t the First Amendment apply to the entire release of emails?**

A. No. Courts have explained that “to properly balance freedom of the press against the right of privacy, every private fact disclosed in an otherwise truthful, newsworthy publication must have some substantial relevance to a matter of legitimate public interest.”_Gilbert v. Med. Econ. Co._, 665 F.2d 305,308(10th Cir. 1981). This rule makes perfect sense in practice. Someone who writes an article about a matter of paramount interest to the public is not entitled to include a social security number in the article (except in the exceedingly rare circumstance that the social security number itself is relevant to the public). A contrary rule would allow anyone to dump on the Internet the contents of the email account of almost anyone engaged in activity of interest to the public, because they could be confident that at least some of the information would be newsworthy.

**Q.****Could your case limit First Amendment protections for journalists?**

A. No. The First Amendment will continue to protect the press because the First Amendment protects the publication of truthful, newsworthy information. A journalist who receives information that is of public interest has the constitutional right to publish that information, even if the journalist’s source obtained it through unlawful means.

**Q. What if a journalist publishes information that she deems newsworthy, but a court disagrees? Would she then be liable?**

A. Almost certainly not. Courts are appropriately reluctant to impose liability on journalists who are simply doing their job. That is why they are enormously deferential to the media’s judgment about what is newsworthy and what is not. This deference ensures that the media has “the breathing space needed . . . for the exercise of effective editorial judgment.”_Virgil v. Time, Inc._, 527 F.2d 1122, 1129 (9th Cir. 1975).

**Q. Would a journalist be liable for publishing newsworthy information that she received from a political campaign in order to harm the campaign’s opponent?**

A. No. As long as the information is newsworthy, the First Amendment protects the right to publish it, regardless of the motives of the source—or even of the journalist. This is what the Supreme Court held in _Bartnicki v. Vopper_, 532 U.S. 514 (2001).

**Q. What if the information was stolen by hackers?**

A. Again, the First Amendment would protect the journalist as long as the information is newsworthy. Of course, if the journalist participated in the hacking or paid the hackers to obtain information the journalist knew had been stolen, she could be liable for participating in the hacking. As journalists know, the First Amendment is not a license to violate generally applicable laws. But as long as the journalist was not involved in the illegal conduct, she is protected by the First Amendment.

# Cockrum, et al. v. Trump for President, Inc.

![Image 1: Keyboard](https://protectdemocracy.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Untitled-design-26.png)Overview
### Overview

Three Americans sued the Trump Campaign for violating their privacy and civil rights.

The plaintiffs are a Reagan-era foreign service officer who grew increasingly worried about the direction of our national politics, a staffer who was making good on a lifelong dream to work in Washington, DC for causes he believed in, and a lottery winner who became a philanthropist to spend his winnings for the greater good.

The complaint alleges that, after Russian hackers stole Democratic National Committee emails, their private information was published to the world as part of a calculated political strategy in which the Trump campaign played a central role. The complaint further alleges that the result was a gross violation of their rights under federal civil rights law, which prohibits conspiracies to injure Americans because of their participation in a presidential election.

No American should fear that the consequence of participating in our democracy is that their identity would be stolen or their personal, private information plastered on the Internet for all to see.

Frequently Asked Questions
### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Didn’t President Trump claim he’d already won this case?**

A:[He did](https://twitter.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1015278594795417600), but as numerous reporters pointed out, he was mistaken. The plaintiffs first filed this case in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia in July 2017. On July 3, 2018, that court dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds, holding that the District of Columbia was “the wrong forum for plaintiffs’ lawsuit.” The Judge went out of her way in issuing that ruling to state: “it bears emphasizing that this Court’s ruling is not based on a finding that there was no collusion between defendants and Russia during the 2016 presidential election.” Protect Democracy disagreed with that ruling, but has now filed the case in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, where the Trump Campaign is incorporated and where therefore the court unquestionably has jurisdiction.

**Q. If some of the leaked information was newsworthy, doesn’t the First Amendment apply to the entire release of emails?**

A. No. Courts have explained that “to properly balance freedom of the press against the right of privacy, every private fact disclosed in an otherwise truthful, newsworthy publication must have some substantial relevance to a matter of legitimate public interest.”_Gilbert v. Med. Econ. Co._, 665 F.2d 305,308(10th Cir. 1981). This rule makes perfect sense in practice. Someone who writes an article about a matter of paramount interest to the public is not entitled to include a social security number in the article (except in the exceedingly rare circumstance that the social security number itself is relevant to the public). A contrary rule would allow anyone to dump on the Internet the contents of the email account of almost anyone engaged in activity of interest to the public, because they could be confident that at least some of the information would be newsworthy.

**Q.****Could your case limit First Amendment protections for journalists?**

A. No. The First Amendment will continue to protect the press because the First Amendment protects the publication of truthful, newsworthy information. A journalist who receives information that is of public interest has the constitutional right to publish that information, even if the journalist’s source obtained it through unlawful means.

**Q. What if a journalist publishes information that she deems newsworthy, but a court disagrees? Would she then be liable?**

A. Almost certainly not. Courts are appropriately reluctant to impose liability on journalists who are simply doing their job. That is why they are enormously deferential to the media’s judgment about what is newsworthy and what is not. This deference ensures that the media has “the breathing space needed . . . for the exercise of effective editorial judgment.”_Virgil v. Time, Inc._, 527 F.2d 1122, 1129 (9th Cir. 1975).

**Q. Would a journalist be liable for publishing newsworthy information that she received from a political campaign in order to harm the campaign’s opponent?**

A. No. As long as the information is newsworthy, the First Amendment protects the right to publish it, regardless of the motives of the source—or even of the journalist. This is what the Supreme Court held in _Bartnicki v. Vopper_, 532 U.S. 514 (2001).

**Q. What if the information was stolen by hackers?**

A. Again, the First Amendment would protect the journalist as long as the information is newsworthy. Of course, if the journalist participated in the hacking or paid the hackers to obtain information the journalist knew had been stolen, she could be liable for participating in the hacking. As journalists know, the First Amendment is not a license to violate generally applicable laws. But as long as the journalist was not involved in the illegal conduct, she is protected by the First Amendment.

What the Experts are Saying
### What the Experts are Saying

##### John McKay, Former Bush-appointed U.S. Attorney, now Partner at Davis Wright Tremaine

“These plaintiffs allege direct harm caused by having their hacked private data published to the world. They make plausible allegations of conspiracy and are entitled to prove these claims. In my experience most conspiracy cases begin with circumstantial evidence just like this case. Investigation and discovery often proves it is true.”

##### Laurence Tr​ibe, Carl M. Loeb University Professor and Professor of Constitutional Law at Harvard Law School

“This powerful new lawsuit offers an excellent prospect of holding the Trump campaign accountable for the severe damage it did to many people’s lives by colluding with the Kremlin to invade and compromise their privacy. The complaints factual allegations are deeply researched and impressively current and the legal theories underlying it are ironclad.”

##### Erwin Chemerinsky, Dean of Berkeley Law

“A civil case only needs to present plausible allegations of harm and a violation of law. That entitles the plaintiffs to discovery to obtain the evidence to prove their claim. The Protect Democracy lawsuit clearly meets these requirements and indeed presents strong claims of wrongdoing.”

##### Benjamin Wittes, editor in chief of Lawfare and a Senior Fellow in Governance Studies at the Brookings Institution, the author of several books, and co-chair of the Hoover Institution’s Working Group on National Security, Technology, and Law

“[T]he case is clearly justiciable and is unlikely to be dismissed on standing grounds. Unlike plaintiffs in a number of other litigations facing Trump right now, there’s no serious standing issue here. The plaintiffs clearly allege that they had their personal information stolen and released and that they suffered real consequences as a result. There’s just no question that this complaint alleges injury in fact or that it seeks relief of a type courts normally grant. What’s more, the case does not present in any sense a political question or a matter that courts are likely to duck.”

##### Vanita Gupta, President and Chief Executive Officer of The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, former Acting Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights

“Federal civil rights laws have played a key role in protecting Americans’ right to freely engage in our democracy for decades. This case is a perfect application of how they should also play a critical role as bulwarks against the kind of voter abuses we’re now facing in the 21st Century. Kudos to Protect Democracy for bringing this important case.”

##### John Nockleby, Professor of Law & Director of the Civil Justice Program at Loyola Law School

“This lawsuit might succeed where others haven’t yet in exposing the Trump campaign’s alleged involvement in disseminating the emails hacked from the servers of the Democratic National Committee… If the lawsuit survives the inevitable motions to dismiss – and it seems to have presented more than enough circumstantial evidence to do so – we may have a window into whether, and if so, exactly how, Trump’s campaign and advisers worked with the government of Russia to sabotage the Clinton campaign, support the Russian government’s agenda, and cause harm to these individual plaintiffs.

##### [Andy Wright](https://www.justsecurity.org/43077/dnc-hack-lawsuit/), Associate Professor at Savannah Law School

“While there are many hurdles to be cleared, this litigation could eventually become a vehicle for discovery of documents and evidence in a judicial proceeding driven by private litigants. That means that a life-tenured federal judge will make determinations based on the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and relevant substantive law without the potential political chokepoints presented by a partisan Congress and compromised Executive.”

##### Jacob W. Buchdahl, Partner at Susman Godfrey L.L.P. and former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York’s public corruption unit

“[I]t’s a circumstantial case, but a compelling one, in light of (a) the numerous contacts between representatives of Russia and the Trump campaign; (b) the repeated falsehoods spread by the Trump campaign regarding those contacts; (c) the accounts (and now-public emails) describing offers of assistance by Russian actors to the Trump campaign; (d) the pro-Russia policy changes advocated by the Trump campaign; and (e) the established involvement by Russia in the hack itself. No plaintiff at the beginning of a lawsuit can point to a written document setting forth the conspirators’ agreement—but what plaintiffs have here is the next best thing.”

##### Jed Shugerman, Professor at Fordham University School of Law

“In Cockrum et al. v. Donald Trump for President, the plaintiffs have solid standing and a firm foundation in a statutory claim: long-standing civil rights law protecting voting rights and privacy from intimidation and harm… Each plaintiff has a compelling story of harm, because the hacking conspiracy released deeply private information or sensitive financial and contact information. The complaint sets out step-by-step the facts suggesting the coordination between Russian hackers and the Trump campaign, and it is actually a riveting weaving of many strands and events over the past year.”

##### Norman Eisen, Chair and Co-Founder, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), former Ambassador the Czech Republic, and Special Counsel to President Obama for Ethics and Government Reform

“This important case seeks justice for ordinary people who were injured in concrete ways by the Russian attack on our democracy. I applaud the plaintiffs for stepping forward to litigate this matter, and their counsel for representing them. I believe the matter will easily survive a motion to dismiss and therefore allow discovery regarding these critically important matters, and I look forward to that.”

# Thompson Issues Statement Following President Trump’s First State of the Union Address

January 30, 2018 

[Press Release](http://thompson.house.gov/media-center/press-releases)

**WASHINGTON D.C. – U.S. Representative Glenn ‘GT’ Thompson tonight issued the following statement at conclusion of President Donald J. Trump’s first State of the Union Address:**

“Tonight, President Trump issued a bold and forward-looking State of the Union address. Thanks to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, this country has just unleashed a new era of economic growth and Americans from all walks of life are beginning to reap the benefits – recognizing lower taxes, more money in their paychecks, and greater potential for domestic businesses investment.   
  
 “As Co-Chair of the House Career and Technical Education Caucus, I was thrilled to hear the President mention his support for greater workforce development and more vocational opportunities. We can work to close the skills gap and put more Americans in family-sustaining jobs. That must start with the Senate passing the bipartisan _Strengthening Career and Technical Education Act for the 21st Century_ _Act_, which passed the House overwhelmingly in June of 2017. I am also pleased that the Democratic response by Rep. Joe Kennedy was delivered from a regional technical school in Massachusetts. Now is the time to do what’s right for the future of the American worker.

“I look forward to the Trump administration, together with Congress and members of both political parties, continuing to work to address many of our greatest challenges.”

**Rep. Thompson**brought his wife,**Mrs. Penny Ammerman Thompson**, as his guest.

How Would Biological Immortality Have Changed the Evolution of Life on Earth?

What would have happened if biological immortality had become widespread among animals during the evolutionary history of life on Earth?

Here, biological immortality means the absence of aging and death from age-related decline, not absolute invulnerability: animals could still die from predators, infections, starvation, injuries, and natural disasters.

For an individual organism, death is the end of life. But in the history of evolution, mortality became one of the factors enabling generational turnover and evolutionary renewal. Paradoxically, the finite lifespans of individual organisms helped make life as a process more resilient to change.

Immortality by itself would not have meant unlimited population growth. Yet a major reduction in mortality would have created a fundamental tension between the lifespan of individuals and the limited carrying capacity of the environment.

Each new generation would add individuals to a population already in existence. If birth rates remained high, population size would quickly approach the limits imposed by available food, water, and territory. Crowding, resource shortages, disease, and intraspecific competition would intensify. In this sense, mortality served as one of the natural checks on overpopulation — an excess of life relative to the carrying capacity of the environment.

Under such conditions, reproduction would come under intense pressure. In many species, energy shortages, chronic stress, and high population density reduce reproductive success. If ecological niches and social positions remained occupied by adult individuals for long periods, younger individuals would also find it more difficult to secure territory, resources, and opportunities to reproduce.

In a population of biologically immortal organisms, maintaining a stable population size would require either that new births be balanced by deaths or emigration, or that reproduction be reduced. The spread of immortality under conditions of limited resources would therefore likely be accompanied by the evolution of mechanisms that sharply restrict reproduction.

An especially important consequence would be a slowdown in generational turnover. Evolution depends on heritable variation, mutations, recombination, and differences in reproductive success. New genetic variants arise and spread across generations. The less frequently generations turn over, the more slowly evolutionary renewal generally proceeds.

Immortality would not stop natural selection: as long as differences in survival and reproduction exist, selection continues to operate. But extreme longevity combined with infrequent reproduction would allow established genotypes to persist for much longer and could slow their replacement by new ones. If the climate changed abruptly, a new pathogen emerged, or another ecological catastrophe occurred, such a population might be less capable of rapid evolutionary adaptation.

There is also an ecological dimension. The death of organisms is an important part of the cycling of matter: decomposition returns carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements to the ecosystem. With a sharp decline in mortality, a substantial share of these elements would remain bound in living biomass for longer, slowing their return to detrital food webs and soil ecosystems. The cycling of matter would not stop completely, since exchange also occurs while organisms are alive, but the structure of ecosystems would change substantially.

Thus, mortality is deeply embedded in the workings of evolution on Earth. It limits overpopulation, frees ecological space, facilitates generational turnover, and plays a role in the cycling of matter. This does not mean that nature deliberately “invented” death for these purposes. Rather, evolution unfolded in a world of mortal organisms, where generational turnover became one of the most important mechanisms of evolutionary renewal.

Here lies a profound paradox: death ends the life of an individual organism, yet the mortality of organisms has contributed to the continuity, capacity for renewal, and adaptability of life as a whole.

Immortality without intelligence and the ability to regulate reproduction, resources, and the state of ecosystems could therefore become not life’s highest victory, but a source of profound crisis.

But with the emergence of intelligence, a new possibility arises. In blind evolution, renewal occurred through generational turnover and the death of individuals. An intelligent civilization could, in principle, try to replace this mechanism with conscious regulation of reproduction, resources, the environment, and its own biological renewal.

Perhaps the central challenge of the future is to preserve individual life while taking over the regulatory and renewal roles that mortality has played for billions of years.

When we think of the most adaptable species, what comes to mind?

Camels are able to survive without food or water for months, cockroaches are said to have survived the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in World War II, and Emperor Penguins are able to make journeys 60+ miles long with their last meal being four months earlier. All of these species are very well suited towards their particular environment, but if one were to put a camel in Antarctica, or an emperor penguin in the Gobi Desert, they would not survive for very long. Adaptability is defined as the ability to adjust oneself readily to different conditions, so while these previously listed species may be able to survive in extreme conditions, they are poorly suited for other environments.

Humans are the most adaptable species on earth which is largely due to our higher intelligence over all other animals. We have reached a point of Supra-Darwinian evolution where ordinary Darwinian evolution has stopped because of our progression of advanced technology and medicine. There is no natural selection or incentive for the human race to continue with Darwinian evolution because technology has made everything easier for us. We don’t have to worry about hunting or gathering because we have grocery stores, and we don’t have to die from otherwise deadly diseases like the flu because we have ways to vaccinate or cure them.

Human’s intelligence has allowed us to live in any environment, which is why humans are one of the only species that can live in 7/7 continents. Given the right technology that we have or can build, humans can live anywhere on earth. We can live in both hot and cold conditions like because we engineered buildings with air conditioning. We have a very diverse diet that consists of many different foods depending on the environment we live in. We have gone to the top of Mt Everest, near the bottom of the deepest part of the ocean, and the moon because we have made the tools to get us there. Our strength and power compared to other animals such as the gorilla have increased due to weapons.

The only creature on earth that would come close to our adaptability would be the Tardigrade, also known as the water bear. These are very small animals (0.05 mm – 1.2 mm long) that can either produce sexually or asexually and prey upon amoeba and even other Tardigrades.

Tardigrades are able to survive insane environments from close to absolute zero, to the pressure that is far greater than the deepest parts of the ocean. What the Tardigrades lack, though, is intelligence which allows humans to form complex social structures and relationships with each other. Social structures are seen in many other primates and species which help them to all hunt better and defend themselves. Humans could not have individually gotten to where we are today without the help from others. Just like the saying goes, Teamwork makes the dream work!

Short answer: Yes — by multiple measures humans are the planet’s most adaptable species, though “adaptable” has dimensions (behavioral, physiological, evolutionary) that change the comparison.

Why humans rank at the top

*   Behavioral flexibility: Humans rapidly invent, learn and transmit new behaviors and technologies across individuals and generations. Cultural transmission (language, teaching, written records, media) lets humans accumulate solutions far faster than genetic evolution.
*   Niche construction: Humans actively modify environments (agriculture, cities, engineered ecosystems) to fit needs rather than solely adapting to preexisting niches. That expands the range of habitable climates and resource regimes.
*   Technological extension: Tools, clothing, controlled fire, housing, medicine, transportation, and climate control allow survival from Arctic tundra to deserts, deep oceans (submersibles), and near-space (satellites, rockets). Technology decouples immediate survival from local physiology.
*   Cognitive generalism: High cognitive plasticity and problem-solving enable flexible foraging, planning, social coordination, and creation of institutions, permitting exploitation of widely different food webs and social ecologies.
*   Demographic and geographic breadth: Humans live on every continent (including permanent settlement in extreme climaxes) and in an extraordinary range of ecosystems simultaneously, showing population-level adaptability rather than isolated specialized populations.

Limits and important caveats

*   Physiological specialization: Many nonhuman species are more physiologically resilient in specific extremes. Polar bears are better adapted to Arctic cold; tardigrades survive extreme desiccation and radiation; psychrophilic microbes thrive in subzero brines humans cannot inhabit without technology.
*   Rapid genetic adaptation: Some organisms (bacteria, viruses, insects) evolve genetically on timescales humans can’t match, acquiring new metabolic capabilities, drug resistance, or tolerance within years or even days. Their evolutionary adaptability can outpace human cultural fixes in certain biological contexts.
*   Dependency on technology and culture: Human adaptability often depends on external systems (energy, infrastructure, supply chains). If technology and knowledge transmission collapse, many human populations would be far less adaptable than many wild species.
*   Ecological impacts and resilience trade-offs: Humans are exceptionally good at altering environments to our advantage, but that creates dependencies (monocultures, urban systems) that can reduce resilience to certain shocks. Other species demonstrate robustness within intact ecosystems.

Useful ways to frame “most adaptable”

*   Short-term behavioral adaptability: humans likely top the list.
*   Long-term genetic evolvability: microbes and rapidly reproducing taxa dominate.
*   Environmental-range occupancy: humans occupy the widest set of macrohabitats via cultural/technological means.
*   Survival without external artifacts: many extremophiles and specialist vertebrates outperform humans.

Examples that illustrate the point

*   Cultural rapid adaptation: introduction of refrigeration, antibiotics, or mobile phones changed human diets, disease patterns, and social organization in decades—changes that no genetic selection could match in speed.
*   Technology enabling habitat expansion: clothing, shelters, and heating allow large human populations to thrive in polar regions; irrigation and crop breeding let agriculture flourish in deserts.
*   Biological counterexample: antibiotic-resistant bacteria evolved resistance within years after antibiotic use began, showing genetic adaptability that rivals or exceeds human capacity to control them.

Conclusion  
Humans are the most adaptable species in behavioral, cultural and technological senses and in breadth of habitat occupancy, but not universally across all definitions. For physiological extremes and fastest genetic adaptation, many microbes, invertebrates and specialist vertebrates outperform humans. The full answer depends on which adaptability metric one emphasizes.

Short answer: no. Scoreboard:

*   [Dinosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur "en.wikipedia.org")—230 million years or more, 10,000 extant genera, worldwide distribution
*   Humans—2 million years, 1 extant genus, one extant species, worldwide distribution aided by technology

Longer answer:

Kids have always loved dinosaurs. When I was a kid, back in the dark ages when dirt was being beta tested, I had a lot of books about dinosaurs, lavishly illustrated. But what those books said about dinosaurs and how they depicted them have changed a lot. In my old books, dinosaurs were presented as reptiles—slow, cold-blooded, and not very smart. Sauropods were always shown standing in swamps because they needed water to help support their weight, and chewing on soft swamp vegetation because they couldn’t chew very well. T-rex was always in a tripod pose, its tail dragging the ground. Much was made of the stupidity of stegosaurus. The books suggested that the dinosaurs went extinct because mammals ate all their eggs, or that they were out-competed by smarter mammals, or that the earth got colder and they, being cold-blooded, simply couldn’t adapt.

![Image 11](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-1d259d9acb35df922ffe2048cc8ec878-pjlq)

Above, from The True Book of Dinosaurs, published in 1955. Below, an old Golden Books cover.

![Image 12](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-56deab7fd37485aa1e6aa42eb8ebbe37-pjlq)

Since then, we’ve learned a lot more about dinosaurs and how they died. We now know that dinosaurs were active. They were warm blooded, with different adaptations to manage body temperature. Many, perhaps most, and maybe even all of them had feathers at some point in their lives. At least some cared for their young. We have found fossil nests with babies well past hatching still living together. Tracks show that in herds, the young were kept in the middle with adults surrounding them.

![Image 13](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-78bb02b93f5650d7effd4b5d0a06467b-pjlq)

Above, the new Golden Books cover, revised with a modern interpretation of dinosaurs.

We know what killed the dinosaurs—the [impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater "en.wikipedia.org") of a massive meteor or something similar that caused worldwide devastation and climate change, roughly 66 million years ago. Almost all land tetrapods over about 55 pounds perished. That is not something that any organism can adapt to. (We would not have.) It would be for any survivors to adapt to the new conditions, evolving and radiating out to fill new ecological niches.

Before this catastrophe, dinosaurs filled almost all of the ecological niches on land. They first diverged from their [archosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archosaur "en.wikipedia.org") forebears during the mid to late Triassic, perhaps as far back as 243 million years ago. They became the dominant land animals following the extinction event that marks the [Triassic-Jurassic boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic%E2%80%93Jurassic_extinction_event "en.wikipedia.org"), 201 million years ago. Our mammalian ancestors were around then. They too made it into the Jurassic, but were confined to relatively few specialty niches, many of them nocturnal. It took a meteor to allow mammals to radiate widely and dominate the large-animal niches.

And some dinosaurs made it through as well! We know them as [birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird "en.wikipedia.org"). Modern birds are descended from small, feathered theropod dinosaurs. True birds, Euornithes, appear in the fossil record in the early Cretaceous. The [most recent common ancestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithurae "en.wikipedia.org") of all [extant modern birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird#Diversification_of_modern_birds "en.wikipedia.org") probably lived in the mid-to-late Cretaceous. There are some 10,000 extant genera of birds, about twice as many as mammalian genera. Dinosaurs continue to be well adapted to life on earth. They’ve been around in some form for well over 230 million years ago. Our genus, [Homo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo "en.wikipedia.org")(humans) has only been around for a little over 2 million years. Anatomically modern humans (Homo sapiens) showed up ~300,000 years ago, with full [behavioral modernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behavioral_modernity "en.wikipedia.org") emerging perhaps as late as 50,000 years ago.

![Image 14](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-7cfdb6482d4ba32f4b1a5a580420e08b-pjlq)

Above, just a few modern dinosaurs.

Our big brains have enabled humans to develop means to survive in places we couldn’t in just our skins. However, our big brains have also enabled us to destroy each other and our own environment in unprecedented ways. We will have to consciously adapt our own behavior if we are to survive. Some birds will probably make it through regardless.

Sweating.  
Seriously.

The most significant difference between humans and our primate cousins is a full-on overhaul of our onboard cooling and heat-management systems. We traded body fur for subcutaneous fat, and could suddenly dump waste heat by evaporation at a maximum rate of 750W!

Along with bipedal running, active cooling enabled early humans to shift ecological niche and become phenomenal endurance hunters. Able to hunt large prey in African temperatures at midday.

This single adaptation also brought with it a significant side-effect.

Once we had this new fangled liquid cooling we could also support a larger brain capacity. Large brains generate a lot of heat, and would cook themselves with old school passive cooling.

So sweating was the key adaptation that allowed us to shift out of the forest, and become cooperative endurance hunters. And that, in turn, brought language, tool use, and the rest.

We are certainly one of the most adaptable vertebrates. “Primitive” humans have adapted to a fairly wide range of earth environments, from some African deserts where the average temperature year round, day and night, is over 30 degrees C to natives of Tierra del Fuego who went with minimal clothing in an area where temperatures rarely get much above freezing. There are human populations that have adapted to altitudes of over 4500 meters in South America. Humans have adapted to some tropical aquatic areas where frequent immersion is a way of life.

Compared with most mammals, we inhabit a much wider range of environments than just about any other critter. The only ones that might give us some competition are our best buddies, dogs, and our nemeses, rats. With dogs, their adaptability has certainly depended on breeding, changing anatomy radically to fit the environment - see samoyeds and salukis.

What has made us even more adaptable is our specialty, behavioral changes - the ability to recognize environmental constraints and do what is necessary to increase our comfort. And our success has crowded out a lot of other animals.

Tough question. We seem to be both extremes at the same time.

We have the intelligence to live in extreme environments, and 8 billion people is a testament to some level of resilience.

However, we’re very reliant on the society, rules and technology that we have built. Without this we are a rather weak species with no decent weapons, no fur to keep us warm, little of the traits that allow us to drink dirty water etc. A few hundred more years of cesareans, glasses, easy access to pharmaceuticals, no need to exercise etc and we will be an even less resilient species, even more dependent on technology.

There is a saying: “I don’t know what World War III will be like, but World War IV will be fought with sticks and stones”.

That’s the idea that if a disaster is big enough that the global economy collapses, we may find ourselves a long way back, maybe even worse than the dark ages. Moreover, we would have none of the easy to extract resources or easy to catch animals that helped us reach civilisation the first time.

We’re riding on a wave, and it isn’t obvious how far we would fall if we fell off it.

How Would Biological Immortality Have Changed the Evolution of Life on Earth?

What would have happened if biological immortality had become widespread among animals during the evolutionary history of life on Earth?

Here, biological immortality means the absence of aging and death from age-related decline, not absolute invulnerability: animals could still die from predators, infections, starvation, injuries, and natural disasters.

For an individual organism, death is the end of life. But in the history of evolution, mortality became one of the factors enabling generational turnover and evolutionary renewal. Paradoxically, the finite lifespans of individual organisms helped make life as a process more resilient to change.

Immortality by itself would not have meant unlimited population growth. Yet a major reduction in mortality would have created a fundamental tension between the lifespan of individuals and the limited carrying capacity of the environment.

Each new generation would add individuals to a population already in existence. If birth rates remained high, population size would quickly approach the limits imposed by available food, water, and territory. Crowding, resource shortages, disease, and intraspecific competition would intensify. In this sense, mortality served as one of the natural checks on overpopulation — an excess of life relative to the carrying capacity of the environment.

Under such conditions, reproduction would come under intense pressure. In many species, energy shortages, chronic stress, and high population density reduce reproductive success. If ecological niches and social positions remained occupied by adult individuals for long periods, younger individuals would also find it more difficult to secure territory, resources, and opportunities to reproduce.

In a population of biologically immortal organisms, maintaining a stable population size would require either that new births be balanced by deaths or emigration, or that reproduction be reduced. The spread of immortality under conditions of limited resources would therefore likely be accompanied by the evolution of mechanisms that sharply restrict reproduction.

An especially important consequence would be a slowdown in generational turnover. Evolution depends on heritable variation, mutations, recombination, and differences in reproductive success. New genetic variants arise and spread across generations. The less frequently generations turn over, the more slowly evolutionary renewal generally proceeds.

Immortality would not stop natural selection: as long as differences in survival and reproduction exist, selection continues to operate. But extreme longevity combined with infrequent reproduction would allow established genotypes to persist for much longer and could slow their replacement by new ones. If the climate changed abruptly, a new pathogen emerged, or another ecological catastrophe occurred, such a population might be less capable of rapid evolutionary adaptation.

There is also an ecological dimension. The death of organisms is an important part of the cycling of matter: decomposition returns carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements to the ecosystem. With a sharp decline in mortality, a substantial share of these elements would remain bound in living biomass for longer, slowing their return to detrital food webs and soil ecosystems. The cycling of matter would not stop completely, since exchange also occurs while organisms are alive, but the structure of ecosystems would change substantially.

Thus, mortality is deeply embedded in the workings of evolution on Earth. It limits overpopulation, frees ecological space, facilitates generational turnover, and plays a role in the cycling of matter. This does not mean that nature deliberately “invented” death for these purposes. Rather, evolution unfolded in a world of mortal organisms, where generational turnover became one of the most important mechanisms of evolutionary renewal.

Here lies a profound paradox: death ends the life of an individual organism, yet the mortality of organisms has contributed to the continuity, capacity for renewal, and adaptability of life as a whole.

Immortality without intelligence and the ability to regulate reproduction, resources, and the state of ecosystems could therefore become not life’s highest victory, but a source of profound crisis.

But with the emergence of intelligence, a new possibility arises. In blind evolution, renewal occurred through generational turnover and the death of individuals. An intelligent civilization could, in principle, try to replace this mechanism with conscious regulation of reproduction, resources, the environment, and its own biological renewal.

Perhaps the central challenge of the future is to preserve individual life while taking over the regulatory and renewal roles that mortality has played for billions of years.

When we think of the most adaptable species, what comes to mind?

Camels are able to survive without food or water for months, cockroaches are said to have survived the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in World War II, and Emperor Penguins are able to make journeys 60+ miles long with their last meal being four months earlier. All of these species are very well suited towards their particular environment, but if one were to put a camel in Antarctica, or an emperor penguin in the Gobi Desert, they would not survive for very long. Adaptability is defined as the ability to adjust oneself readily to different conditions, so while these previously listed species may be able to survive in extreme conditions, they are poorly suited for other environments.

Humans are the most adaptable species on earth which is largely due to our higher intelligence over all other animals. We have reached a point of Supra-Darwinian evolution where ordinary Darwinian evolution has stopped because of our progression of advanced technology and medicine. There is no natural selection or incentive for the human race to continue with Darwinian evolution because technology has made everything easier for us. We don’t have to worry about hunting or gathering because we have grocery stores, and we don’t have to die from otherwise deadly diseases like the flu because we have ways to vaccinate or cure them.

Human’s intelligence has allowed us to live in any environment, which is why humans are one of the only species that can live in 7/7 continents. Given the right technology that we have or can build, humans can live anywhere on earth. We can live in both hot and cold conditions like because we engineered buildings with air conditioning. We have a very diverse diet that consists of many different foods depending on the environment we live in. We have gone to the top of Mt Everest, near the bottom of the deepest part of the ocean, and the moon because we have made the tools to get us there. Our strength and power compared to other animals such as the gorilla have increased due to weapons.

The only creature on earth that would come close to our adaptability would be the Tardigrade, also known as the water bear. These are very small animals (0.05 mm – 1.2 mm long) that can either produce sexually or asexually and prey upon amoeba and even other Tardigrades.

Tardigrades are able to survive insane environments from close to absolute zero, to the pressure that is far greater than the deepest parts of the ocean. What the Tardigrades lack, though, is intelligence which allows humans to form complex social structures and relationships with each other. Social structures are seen in many other primates and species which help them to all hunt better and defend themselves. Humans could not have individually gotten to where we are today without the help from others. Just like the saying goes, Teamwork makes the dream work!

Short answer: Yes — by multiple measures humans are the planet’s most adaptable species, though “adaptable” has dimensions (behavioral, physiological, evolutionary) that change the comparison.

Why humans rank at the top

*   Behavioral flexibility: Humans rapidly invent, learn and transmit new behaviors and technologies across individuals and generations. Cultural transmission (language, teaching, written records, media) lets humans accumulate solutions far faster than genetic evolution.
*   Niche construction: Humans actively modify environments (agriculture, cities, engineered ecosystems) to fit needs rather than solely adapting to preexisting niches. That expands the range of habitable climates and resource regimes.
*   Technological extension: Tools, clothing, controlled fire, housing, medicine, transportation, and climate control allow survival from Arctic tundra to deserts, deep oceans (submersibles), and near-space (satellites, rockets). Technology decouples immediate survival from local physiology.
*   Cognitive generalism: High cognitive plasticity and problem-solving enable flexible foraging, planning, social coordination, and creation of institutions, permitting exploitation of widely different food webs and social ecologies.
*   Demographic and geographic breadth: Humans live on every continent (including permanent settlement in extreme climaxes) and in an extraordinary range of ecosystems simultaneously, showing population-level adaptability rather than isolated specialized populations.

Limits and important caveats

*   Physiological specialization: Many nonhuman species are more physiologically resilient in specific extremes. Polar bears are better adapted to Arctic cold; tardigrades survive extreme desiccation and radiation; psychrophilic microbes thrive in subzero brines humans cannot inhabit without technology.
*   Rapid genetic adaptation: Some organisms (bacteria, viruses, insects) evolve genetically on timescales humans can’t match, acquiring new metabolic capabilities, drug resistance, or tolerance within years or even days. Their evolutionary adaptability can outpace human cultural fixes in certain biological contexts.
*   Dependency on technology and culture: Human adaptability often depends on external systems (energy, infrastructure, supply chains). If technology and knowledge transmission collapse, many human populations would be far less adaptable than many wild species.
*   Ecological impacts and resilience trade-offs: Humans are exceptionally good at altering environments to our advantage, but that creates dependencies (monocultures, urban systems) that can reduce resilience to certain shocks. Other species demonstrate robustness within intact ecosystems.

Useful ways to frame “most adaptable”

*   Short-term behavioral adaptability: humans likely top the list.
*   Long-term genetic evolvability: microbes and rapidly reproducing taxa dominate.
*   Environmental-range occupancy: humans occupy the widest set of macrohabitats via cultural/technological means.
*   Survival without external artifacts: many extremophiles and specialist vertebrates outperform humans.

Examples that illustrate the point

*   Cultural rapid adaptation: introduction of refrigeration, antibiotics, or mobile phones changed human diets, disease patterns, and social organization in decades—changes that no genetic selection could match in speed.
*   Technology enabling habitat expansion: clothing, shelters, and heating allow large human populations to thrive in polar regions; irrigation and crop breeding let agriculture flourish in deserts.
*   Biological counterexample: antibiotic-resistant bacteria evolved resistance within years after antibiotic use began, showing genetic adaptability that rivals or exceeds human capacity to control them.

Conclusion  
Humans are the most adaptable species in behavioral, cultural and technological senses and in breadth of habitat occupancy, but not universally across all definitions. For physiological extremes and fastest genetic adaptation, many microbes, invertebrates and specialist vertebrates outperform humans. The full answer depends on which adaptability metric one emphasizes.

Short answer: no. Scoreboard:

*   [Dinosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur "en.wikipedia.org")—230 million years or more, 10,000 extant genera, worldwide distribution
*   Humans—2 million years, 1 extant genus, one extant species, worldwide distribution aided by technology

Longer answer:

Kids have always loved dinosaurs. When I was a kid, back in the dark ages when dirt was being beta tested, I had a lot of books about dinosaurs, lavishly illustrated. But what those books said about dinosaurs and how they depicted them have changed a lot. In my old books, dinosaurs were presented as reptiles—slow, cold-blooded, and not very smart. Sauropods were always shown standing in swamps because they needed water to help support their weight, and chewing on soft swamp vegetation because they couldn’t chew very well. T-rex was always in a tripod pose, its tail dragging the ground. Much was made of the stupidity of stegosaurus. The books suggested that the dinosaurs went extinct because mammals ate all their eggs, or that they were out-competed by smarter mammals, or that the earth got colder and they, being cold-blooded, simply couldn’t adapt.

![Image 11](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-1d259d9acb35df922ffe2048cc8ec878-pjlq)

Above, from The True Book of Dinosaurs, published in 1955. Below, an old Golden Books cover.

![Image 12](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-56deab7fd37485aa1e6aa42eb8ebbe37-pjlq)

Since then, we’ve learned a lot more about dinosaurs and how they died. We now know that dinosaurs were active. They were warm blooded, with different adaptations to manage body temperature. Many, perhaps most, and maybe even all of them had feathers at some point in their lives. At least some cared for their young. We have found fossil nests with babies well past hatching still living together. Tracks show that in herds, the young were kept in the middle with adults surrounding them.

![Image 13](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-78bb02b93f5650d7effd4b5d0a06467b-pjlq)

Above, the new Golden Books cover, revised with a modern interpretation of dinosaurs.

We know what killed the dinosaurs—the [impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater "en.wikipedia.org") of a massive meteor or something similar that caused worldwide devastation and climate change, roughly 66 million years ago. Almost all land tetrapods over about 55 pounds perished. That is not something that any organism can adapt to. (We would not have.) It would be for any survivors to adapt to the new conditions, evolving and radiating out to fill new ecological niches.

Before this catastrophe, dinosaurs filled almost all of the ecological niches on land. They first diverged from their [archosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archosaur "en.wikipedia.org") forebears during the mid to late Triassic, perhaps as far back as 243 million years ago. They became the dominant land animals following the extinction event that marks the [Triassic-Jurassic boundary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic%E2%80%93Jurassic_extinction_event "en.wikipedia.org"), 201 million years ago. Our mammalian ancestors were around then. They too made it into the Jurassic, but were confined to relatively few specialty niches, many of them nocturnal. It took a meteor to allow mammals to radiate widely and dominate the large-animal niches.

And some dinosaurs made it through as well! We know them as [birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird "en.wikipedia.org"). Modern birds are descended from small, feathered theropod dinosaurs. True birds, Euornithes, appear in the fossil record in the early Cretaceous. The [most recent common ancestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithurae "en.wikipedia.org") of all [extant modern birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird#Diversification_of_modern_birds "en.wikipedia.org") probably lived in the mid-to-late Cretaceous. There are some 10,000 extant genera of birds, about twice as many as mammalian genera. Dinosaurs continue to be well adapted to life on earth. They’ve been around in some form for well over 230 million years ago. Our genus, [Homo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo "en.wikipedia.org")(humans) has only been around for a little over 2 million years. Anatomically modern humans (Homo sapiens) showed up ~300,000 years ago, with full [behavioral modernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behavioral_modernity "en.wikipedia.org") emerging perhaps as late as 50,000 years ago.

![Image 14](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-7cfdb6482d4ba32f4b1a5a580420e08b-pjlq)

Above, just a few modern dinosaurs.

Our big brains have enabled humans to develop means to survive in places we couldn’t in just our skins. However, our big brains have also enabled us to destroy each other and our own environment in unprecedented ways. We will have to consciously adapt our own behavior if we are to survive. Some birds will probably make it through regardless.

Sweating.  
Seriously.

The most significant difference between humans and our primate cousins is a full-on overhaul of our onboard cooling and heat-management systems. We traded body fur for subcutaneous fat, and could suddenly dump waste heat by evaporation at a maximum rate of 750W!

Along with bipedal running, active cooling enabled early humans to shift ecological niche and become phenomenal endurance hunters. Able to hunt large prey in African temperatures at midday.

This single adaptation also brought with it a significant side-effect.

Once we had this new fangled liquid cooling we could also support a larger brain capacity. Large brains generate a lot of heat, and would cook themselves with old school passive cooling.

So sweating was the key adaptation that allowed us to shift out of the forest, and become cooperative endurance hunters. And that, in turn, brought language, tool use, and the rest.

We are certainly one of the most adaptable vertebrates. “Primitive” humans have adapted to a fairly wide range of earth environments, from some African deserts where the average temperature year round, day and night, is over 30 degrees C to natives of Tierra del Fuego who went with minimal clothing in an area where temperatures rarely get much above freezing. There are human populations that have adapted to altitudes of over 4500 meters in South America. Humans have adapted to some tropical aquatic areas where frequent immersion is a way of life.

Compared with most mammals, we inhabit a much wider range of environments than just about any other critter. The only ones that might give us some competition are our best buddies, dogs, and our nemeses, rats. With dogs, their adaptability has certainly depended on breeding, changing anatomy radically to fit the environment - see samoyeds and salukis.

What has made us even more adaptable is our specialty, behavioral changes - the ability to recognize environmental constraints and do what is necessary to increase our comfort. And our success has crowded out a lot of other animals.

Tough question. We seem to be both extremes at the same time.

We have the intelligence to live in extreme environments, and 8 billion people is a testament to some level of resilience.

However, we’re very reliant on the society, rules and technology that we have built. Without this we are a rather weak species with no decent weapons, no fur to keep us warm, little of the traits that allow us to drink dirty water etc. A few hundred more years of cesareans, glasses, easy access to pharmaceuticals, no need to exercise etc and we will be an even less resilient species, even more dependent on technology.

There is a saying: “I don’t know what World War III will be like, but World War IV will be fought with sticks and stones”.

That’s the idea that if a disaster is big enough that the global economy collapses, we may find ourselves a long way back, maybe even worse than the dark ages. Moreover, we would have none of the easy to extract resources or easy to catch animals that helped us reach civilisation the first time.

We’re riding on a wave, and it isn’t obvious how far we would fall if we fell off it.

How Would Biological Immortality Have Changed the Evolution of Life on Earth?

What would have happened if biological immortality had become widespread among animals during the evolutionary history of life on Earth?

Here, biological immortality means the absence of aging and death from age-related decline, not absolute invulnerability: animals could still die from predators, infections, starvation, injuries, and natural disasters.

For an individual organism, death is the end of life. But in the history of evolution, mortality became one of the factors enabling generational turnover and evolutionary renewal. Paradoxically, the finite lifespans of individual organisms helped make life as a process more resilient to change.

Immortality by itself would not have meant unlimited population growth. Yet a major reduction in mortality would have created a fundamental tension between the lifespan of individuals and the limited carrying capacity of the environment.

Each new generation would add individuals to a population already in existence. If birth rates remained high, population size would quickly approach the limits imposed by available food, water, and territory. Crowding, resource shortages, disease, and intraspecific competition would intensify. In this sense, mortality served as one of the natural checks on overpopulation — an excess of life relative to the carrying capacity of the environment.

Under such conditions, reproduction would come under intense pressure. In many species, energy shortages, chronic stress, and high population density reduce reproductive success. If ecological niches and social positions remained occupied by adult individuals for long periods, younger individuals would also find it more difficult to secure territory, resources, and opportunities to reproduce.

In a population of biologically immortal organisms, maintaining a stable population size would require either that new births be balanced by deaths or emigration, or that reproduction be reduced. The spread of immortality under conditions of limited resources would therefore likely be accompanied by the evolution of mechanisms that sharply restrict reproduction.

An especially important consequence would be a slowdown in generational turnover. Evolution depends on heritable variation, mutations, recombination, and differences in reproductive success. New genetic variants arise and spread across generations. The less frequently generations turn over, the more slowly evolutionary renewal generally proceeds.

Immortality would not stop natural selection: as long as differences in survival and reproduction exist, selection continues to operate. But extreme longevity combined with infrequent reproduction would allow established genotypes to persist for much longer and could slow their replacement by new ones. If the climate changed abruptly, a new pathogen emerged, or another ecological catastrophe occurred, such a population might be less capable of rapid evolutionary adaptation.

There is also an ecological dimension. The death of organisms is an important part of the cycling of matter: decomposition returns carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements to the ecosystem. With a sharp decline in mortality, a substantial share of these elements would remain bound in living biomass for longer, slowing their return to detrital food webs and soil ecosystems. The cycling of matter would not stop completely, since exchange also occurs while organisms are alive, but the structure of ecosystems would change substantially.

Thus, mortality is deeply embedded in the workings of evolution on Earth. It limits overpopulation, frees ecological space, facilitates generational turnover, and plays a role in the cycling of matter. This does not mean that nature deliberately “invented” death for these purposes. Rather, evolution unfolded in a world of mortal organisms, where generational turnover became one of the most important mechanisms of evolutionary renewal.

Here lies a profound paradox: death ends the life of an individual organism, yet the mortality of organisms has contributed to the continuity, capacity for renewal, and adaptability of life as a whole.

Immortality without intelligence and the ability to regulate reproduction, resources, and the state of ecosystems could therefore become not life’s highest victory, but a source of profound crisis.

But with the emergence of intelligence, a new possibility arises. In blind evolution, renewal occurred through generational turnover and the death of individuals. An intelligent civilization could, in principle, try to replace this mechanism with conscious regulation of reproduction, resources, the environment, and its own biological renewal.

Perhaps the central challenge of the future is to preserve individual life while taking over the regulatory and renewal roles that mortality has played for billions of years.

My somewhat cheat-y answer is the animals that have adapted to living in human habitations—cities and homes. That gives them a stable environment that’s pretty resistant to changes in the overall climate.

So…cockroaches, bedbugs, rats and mice…critters like that.

But there are also animals that live outdoors but happily dwell in cities, which still protects them to a degree from climate changes. Raccoons, skunks, crows, pigeons, peregrine falcons (they love cities—high rises to nest on and pigeons to feed on…kind of a paradise for them). Crows favor open woodlands, which equals city parks and urban landscaping in general. Where I Iive, in a big condo complex, they arrived a few decades ago and have gradually pushed out songbirds like robins.

In all these cases it’s less that the animal has adapted—6K years is pretty short for that with most animal species—than that our habitats match up—from their point of view—pretty well with what they had slowly evolved to live in.

By the end of the Mozambican Civil War, the local elephant population had plummeted by 90 percent. But the survivors shared a bizarre, life-saving anomaly: half of the females had no tusks.

For African elephants, tusks are essential tools used to dig for water, strip bark from trees, and defend against predators. However, during the conflict from 1977 to 1992, the environment in Gorongosa National Park changed from a protected habitat into a deadly war zone. Armed forces on both sides of the war relied heavily on the ivory trade to finance their operations, aggressively poaching elephants. This intense hunting pressure essentially turned a natural survival advantage into a lethal liability.

Prior to the conflict, approximately 18.5 percent of female elephants in the region were naturally tuskless, representing a relatively rare genetic quirk. But as poachers systematically eliminated elephants with tusks, those without them were left to survive and reproduce. By the time the war ended, 50 percent of the surviving females were tuskless. Even more remarkably, 33 percent of the female elephants born in the generation immediately following the war never grew tusks at all.

Biologists studying the Gorongosa elephants discovered that this rapid shift was not a random anomaly, but a clear case of human-driven evolution. The trait for tusklessness is tied to a specific dominant genetic mutation on the X chromosome. Interestingly, this mutation is lethal to male calves in the womb, meaning the adaptation exclusively affects females. The surviving tuskless mothers passed this life-saving gene to their daughters, completely altering the physical profile of the herd in just a few decades.

This phenomenon highlights exactly how quickly extreme environmental pressures can force a species to pivot. In the span of a single generation, the elephants of Mozambique biologically rewired their anatomy to survive a landscape defined by the ivory trade.

In parts of East Africa, people use special calls to summon a wild bird—and it leads them to hidden bee nests they would struggle to find alone.

One of the best examples is the partnership between honeyguide birds and humans in parts of East Africa. It sounds almost folkloric, but it is a real, well-documented case of two very different species cooperating to deal with a difficult resource: wild bee nests.

Finding honey in a hot, dry landscape is hard enough. Getting it out is worse. Bee colonies hide inside tree cavities or underground hollows, and the bees defend them aggressively. Neither partner is especially well equipped to solve the whole problem alone:

*   The greater honeyguide is excellent at locating nests.
*   Human honey hunters are good at opening nests and controlling the bees with smoke.
*   Both get food that would otherwise be much harder to obtain.

The sequence is remarkably specific. In regions of Mozambique, Tanzania, and Kenya, honey hunters use special calls to attract honeyguides. The bird responds, then flies from tree to tree, giving calls and waiting for the humans to follow. Once the nest is found, people use tools and smoke to break into it and harvest the honey. After the humans leave, the bird feeds on what remains—especially wax, bee larvae, and scraps from the hive.

That last detail matters. Honeyguides are among the very few birds able to digest beeswax efficiently. So this is not just opportunism at the edge of human activity; the bird is exploiting a food source that becomes accessible mainly because of the partnership.

What makes this especially interesting is that it appears to be a case of mutual adaptation shaped by culture and evolution at the same time:

1.   Humans learned signals and calls that improve the chance of recruiting a bird.
2.   Birds learned to recognize and respond to those calls.
3.   In some communities, this behavior became a stable tradition passed across generations.

Field studies have shown that traditional honey-hunting calls can significantly increase the probability of being led to a nest. In other words, this is not a charming anecdote; it measurably improves foraging success in a harsh environment where calories are valuable and resources are patchy.

There are many other examples of animals cooperating across species—reef fish cleaning larger fish, oxpeckers associating with big mammals, coyotes and badgers hunting together—but the honeyguide-human relationship is unusual because it combines:

*   wild animal cognition,
*   human cultural knowledge,
*   communication across species,
*   and survival in an environment where neither side has the full toolkit alone.

It is a reminder that adaptation is not always about growing thicker fur or sharper teeth. Sometimes it is about learning how to read another species well enough that both sides come out ahead.

If by “evolve,” you mean by the “theory of evolution” aka the “modern synthesis” aka neo-Darwinism, no. It takes millions of year's. One scientist calculated for a pair of sequential beneficial mutations to occur would take 9 million years.

Problem is folks sling the word evolution around as if it means the “theory of evolution.” It doesn't. It simply means change over time which includes the “theory of evolution”—big difference.

Now the new theory of evolution or rather “change” (epigenetics) is different from neo-Darwinism as it causes rapid “evolution” or rather “change” or “adaptation” by changing the way DNA is “read” without neo-Darwinian mutations. Indeed epigenetics does not mutate the DNA rather it places methyl “tags” on the DNA which are reversable. Depending on the environment they can cause rapid adaptation of the organism. This is not natural selection as NS as definition for 60 years claimed a “random” mutation must occur and NS fixes it in the DNA.

This hasn't stopped many scientists, that realise the old natural selection is defunct, from trying to apply NS to epigenetics. But again there are hundreds of thousands of articles claiming the old NS is right. They can't ignore this.

Epigenetics works 10,000 as fast as natural selection mutations. As such we can observe their “change” within one generation. Identical twin studies are a remarkable example. One twin might be schizophrenic while the other is not. Scientists account this to epigenetics.

There are a growing amount of examples of this. Over the last 10 years there have been 122,000 articles on epigenetics whereas only 179 on the “theory of evolution” aka the “modern synthesis.”

For example everyone knows Darwin had his epiphany on the Beagle studying the Finches. There are over 18,000 articles on it trying to concord their mutational changes with neodarwinism yet “no joy.”

Yet these authors explored the epigenetic differences to great success. They say,

“The prevailing theory for the molecular basis of evolution involves genetic MUTATIONS that ultimately generate the heritable phenotypic variation on which natural selection acts

However, EPIGENETICS… plays an important role in evolutionary change.

Genome-wide alterations in genetic mutations using copy number variation (CNV) were compared with epigenetic alterations associated with differential DNA methylation regions (epimutations)

Epimutations were MORE COMMON than genetic CNV mutations among the five species

The number of genetic CNV mutations DID NOT consistently increase with phylogenetic distance. (Mutations did not align with the phenotype or body type)

The number, chromosomal locations, regional clustering, and LACK OF OVERLAP of…GENETIC MUTATIONS suggest that EPIGENETIC changes are distinct and that they CORRELATE with the evolutionary history of Darwin’s finch es.”
