# 5. Management Actions 

Management actions have been developed to address the potential threats identified in Chapter 3 and the goals and objectives identified in Chapter 4. These management actions should be carried out over the first 10 years after plan adoption. The actions should maintain or improve the ecological condition of the Reserve and will assist in the adaptive management process that will occur after the first 10 years of plan implementation. Because the management actions in this plan will take several years to implement, actions have been prioritized to identify those that should be completed sooner versus those that may be completed in late as time and resources permit. Actions that should be initially undertaken, preferably within the first five years, are identified as tier one, and actions that may be initiated as time and resources permit, are identified as tier two. DNR actions related to use authorizations are considered tier one and should be implemented throughout the 90-year period or until amended through adaptive management processes. This prioritization is based upon the analysis of risks and the future desired conditions of the plan, and should be periodically revisited as our understanding of the relationship between ecological processes, anthropogenic stressors, and species or habitat conditions decline at the Reserve improves. DNR will use this plan to guide decisions regarding authorizations for uses of state-owned aquatic lands within and directly adjacent to the aquatic reserve. The management emphasis for new authorizations on state-owned lands will place protection of native aquatic habitats above all other management actions. For existing uses located on state-owned aquatic lands directly adjacent to the reserve, the focus will be to reduce their existing impacts over the 90-year time frame of the reserve. Since impacts to sensitive habitats and species within the reserve may also be attributed to activities that DNR does not have explicit authority to manage, such as upland uses, DNR will seek management cooperation and collaboration from others resource management agencies. DNR will work with regulatory agencies, tribes and others to ensure that existing, future uses and activities contribute to the management goals of this plan. The management actions for the Cherry Point Aquatic Reserve focus on protection and restoration of sensitive aquatic resources in the context of planning for existing, future industrial, recreational, stewardship, and cultural uses of state-owned lands. The actions are grouped under six categories: 

 Conservation of Ecosystems, Habitats and Species 

 Restoration and Enhancement 

 Outreach and Education 

 Monitoring, Data Collection, and Research 

 Allowed Uses

# Monitoring, Data Collection and Research 

There are four components of research and monitoring within the reserve: 

 Data gap analysis Washington State Department of Natural Resources ▪ Cherry Point Aquatic Reserve Management Plan ▪ 43 

 Establishing baseline conditions 

 Trend monitoring to determine the effectiveness of management activities and document natural variation; and 

 Research to better understand observed changes and the interactions between management activities and natural resource conditions. 

Data gap analysis will help managers determine baseline conditions that represent the current quality of the Cherry Point ecosystem. These conditions set the baseline for monitoring ecosystem health to which future conditions will be compared in order to judge progress and effectiveness. Baseline monitoring will document current conditions by combining existing data with new characterizations of resources and ecological processes proposed in this plan. After baseline conditions have been identified, continued monitoring for trends in habitat and species conditions should be conducted. Trend monitoring will be used to assess the success of management actions in attaining or exceeding the goals identified previously in this management plan. Trend monitoring is necessary in order to assess the need for course corrections related to improving the management actions. Research can compliment trend monitoring by providing possible answers for why species and habitats may be declining or improving. Because there are many management actions related to data collection, monitoring and research, the following actions are a high priority over the first five years of plan implementation: 1) monitoring the effectiveness of protection actions that address existing and proposed use authorizations, and 2) research to reduce uncertainties about the decline of species targeted for conservation that can directly improve the effectiveness of management actions.

[PDF page 1]
FINAL

ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT

30 April 1971

Salt Creek Lake, Salt Creek, Scioto River Basin, Ohio

(  )  Draft  (X)  Final Environmental Statement

Responsible Office:  U. S. Army Engineer District, Huntington,
West Virginia

1.  Marne of Action:  (X)  Administrative  (  )  Legislative

2.  Description of Action:  Construction and operation of a dam and
other reservoir facilities for flood control, outdoor recreation,
and fish and wildlife enhancement, with incidental beneficial effects
for redevelopment and low-flow regulation.

3.  a.  Environmental Impacts;  Conversion of a reach of non-regulated
stream to a lake-type habitat, regulation of downstream flood and low
flows, and change of land use in the project area.

b.  Adverse Environmental Effects:  Disruption of private and
communal environments of individuals and groups now using the lands
to be acquired, loss of some timberland and agricultural land, and
loss of certain types of biotic habitat.

4.  Alternatives:  Single-purpose developments or combinations of
developments to provide equivalent services such as reservoirs with
similar storage capacities; local flood protection works; non-struc-
tural flood damage techniques such as zoning and floodproofing;
recreational development of the stream; more intensive recreational
development elsewhere; no action.

5.  Comments Received:

Public Health Service, HEW (now Environmental Protection Agency)
Ohio Historical Society
Federal Water Quality Administration, EPA (now Water Quality Office)
National Park Service, USDI
Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, FSWS, USDI
Eastern Region, Forest Service, USDA
Northeastern Area, Statute £ Private Forestry, Forest Service, USDA
Ohio Department of Natural Resources (including Dept, of Health)
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, USDI
Ohio Conservation Foundation (with conments from the Asst. Curator
of the Museum of Zoology of Ohio State Univ.)

6.  Draft statement to CEQ  " ^ ^
Final statement to CEQ  g  8  OCT  1971

[PDF page 3]
SALT CREEK LAKE

1.  Project description.  The Salt Creek Lake project will con­
sist of the construction and operation of a dam and other facilities
for flood control, recreation, and fish and wildlife enhancement, with
incidental redevelopment benefits.  The Salt Creek Lake is one unit in
the comprehensive plan for water resources development of the Scioto
River Basin.  The plan consists of seven major reservoir projects
(two are operational, two under construction, and the other three in
planning and design), one local protection project,  and one channel
improvement project.  Project formulation and system analysis are dis­
cussed in House Document No.  587 of the 87th Congress, 2nd Session.
The dam is to be located in Ross County, Ohio, on Salt Creek, 10.8
miles above its confluence with Scioto River.  It will regulate the
runoff from a 285 square mile watershed.  As presently planned, the
pool to be maintained will be at elevation 625.0 feet above mean sea
level, will have a surface area of about 1,233 acres, and a shoreline
length of about 23 miles;  storage capacity of 94,002 acre-feet will be
available for temporary impoundment of water during flood periods.
The larger part of the reservoir will be in Vinton County, but it will
extend into Hocking County.  The project, authorized by the Flood Con­
trol Act of 1962, currently Is in the advanced engineering and design
stage.  Its benefit-to-cost ratio is 1.15 to 1.

2.  Environmental setting without the project.  The Salt Creek
Lake project site is in the Appalachian Region, and in the vicinity
many of the social and economic problems typical of Appalachia are
evident.  Ross County (which is on the periphery of Appalachia and
straddles the Scioto River valley, with its attendant transportation,
industry, and agriculture)  is one of the richest counties in Appalachian
Ohio.  On the other hand, Vinton County, which contains the major por­
tion of the area to be acquired for the project,  is one of the more
depressed counties in Ohio.  In both counties, however, in comparison
with the State as a whole and with the Nation, the'population is rela­
tively sparse and is declining, the level of education is low, family
income is low, housing conditions are poor, and per capita property
taxes are low.  Nevertheless, in June 1970, unemployment was 4.0 per­
cent in Ross County and 4.3 percent in Vinton County, these rates being
close to the average for State and Nation.

The reservoir site is in the unglaciated Kanawha Section of
the Appalachian Plateau physiographic province, an area of maturely
dissected topography.  Total relief in the project area is about 500
feet, and the hillsides are frequently steep.  In the project area,
Salt Creek has formed a relativelv broad, alluvial plain, averaging
about half a mile wide.  The cleared and cultivated areas of the farms
occupy the valley floors and extend up over the toes of the hills.
The tipper slopes are densely forested.

[PDF page 4]
Salt Creek heads in a ground moraine within the southeastern
edge of the glaciated portion of central Ohio.  From there it flows
generally southward through relatively level, glaciated terrain, then
turns southwest and flows in a deeply entrenched valley through rugged,
unglaciated terrain to its confluence with the Scioto, downriver from
Chillicothe.  The stream gradient averages about 10 feet to the mile.
In the project reach, Salt Creek is underlain by as much as 80 feet of
alluvium, as it traverses a series of silted pools interrupted by sand,
gravel, and rubble riffles.

The average annual flow of Salt Creek at the dam site is 300
cubic feet per second, varying from a March normal average of 738 c.f.s.
to an October normal average of 26 c.f.s.  Minimum average flow for a
month has dropped below 8 c.f.s. and instantaneous low flows have been
recorded at less than 5 c.f.s., while brief flood flow has exceeded
34,000 c.f.s.

Flood flows from Salt Creek contribute to the damage of
several towns along the Scioto River (Higby, Waverly, Piketon, and
Lucasville) and to towns and industries along the Ohio River.  Recurring
flooding along the reach of Salt Creek downstream from the project makes
the land there undesirable for industrial development, notwithstanding
that it is level, and well served by highways and railroads.

Frequent natural low flows restrict assimilative capacity
thereby affecting productivity of the fishery and the aesthetic appeal
of the stream.

Salt Creek in its present condition supports good to excellent
populations of muskellunge, channel catfish,  shovelhead catfish, small-
mouth bass, spotted bass, rock bass, sunfish, and rough fish.  Stream
fishing is of importance in this section of Ohio, as practically no
reservoir fishing is available.  Private owners of lands adjoining the
project reach of Salt Creek permit public use of the stream, which re­
sults in heavy fishing pressure.  Average annual fisherman-use on Salt
Creek within and downstream from the project area is about 960 man-days
of fishing per mile.

Salt Creek has waterfowl resource value in providing good duck
nesting and resting areas.  Black and mallard ducks use the area occa­
sionally.  Hunter use is estimated at the average annual rate of one
hunter-day per mile of stream.  Fair populations of muskrat and mink
occur along Salt Creek.

The valley floor is largely farm-game habitat, supporting
primarily rabbits, quail, raccoon, and songbirds.  In the forested hills
white-tailed deer, fox, gray squirrels, ruffed grouse, and turkey are
present.  Fox hunting and raccoon hunting with dogs are popular sports.
Average annual hunting use is estimated at 112 man-days per square mile.

[PDF page 5]
3.  The environmental impact of the proposed action.  The proposed
project will provide water storage which will be used for flood control,
general recreation, and fish and wildlife recreation.  Along with the
effects resulting directly from these major intended purposes,  there
will be nunerous effects on the environment resulting from the processes
initiated by the project.

The amount of water released from the dam will be regulated
so as to decrease peak flow.  This will alleviate the recurring, destruc­
tive floods along the Scioto River and contribute to the reduction of
flooding on the Ohio River.  Monetary savings attributable to flood
reduction are expected to average $740,000 annually.  Intangible effects
will include reduced possibility of death,  injury, or illness resulting
from floods; reduction of the social and economic insecurity caused by
frequent flooding; lessening of the necessity to commit labor and mate­
rial to emergency and relief operations; and reduced aesthetic degrada­
tion of communities subject to floods.  Incidental effects of flood re­
duction include a decrease  in the competence of the stream to transport
larger particles, possibly resulting in a change in the hydraulic and
biologic characteristics of the riverbed.

The flood protection resulting from the project will increase
the attractiveness of the land downstream and will change existing land-
use patterns.  The land will probably be converted to a higher economic
use, with mare residences and mare businesses.  Several parcels of land
near Londonderry presently have limited potential for industrial and
commercial use.  Existence of the reservoir will, however, foster the
growth of the community, and the economic potential of the land will
be increased by reason of reservoir-related activities.

The dam will regulate the base flow of the stream so that from
April through November it does not drop below 20 c.f.s., and for the
remainder of the year below 10 c.f.s.  This regulation will prevent
periods of extreme low flow such as occur under normal (unregulated)
conditions and thus will increase the ability of the stream (and the
Scioto River) to assimilate pollutants.  In addition to treated and
industrial and municipal wastes, pollutants enter the streams from
normal bank erosion and from runoff or drainage from agricultural lands
and developed areas thereby involving such contaminents as sediment,
fertilizers, pesticides, herbicides, and chemicals or salts used for
ice and snow control.  Augmentation of low flows also will increase the
capacity of the stream to support some types of aquatic life and riparian
vegetation, will maintain the visual character of the stream by prevent­
ing its "going dry"  in the fall, and will help maintain water quality
standards along the lower reaches of the Scioto River.

[PDF page 6]
A 1,233-acre recreation pool with a capacity of 11,462 acre-
feet will be maintained at elevation 625 throughout the year except
when detained flood waters raise the level or when, on rare occasions,
the minimum release exceeds the inflow and the level is lowered.  The
pool will be relatively stable and, therefore,  is expected to develop
an ecosystem similar to that of a natural lake.  Reservoir clearing
will be coordinated with state officials to facilitate fish and wildlife
management.  The lake will provide permanent habitat for water-associated
mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and birds, as well as fish.  The U. S.
Fish and Wildlife Service indicates that the,relative stability of the
pool will be conducive to the establishment of permanent populations
of life forms that will increase the opportunity to enjoy non-consumptive
use of wildlife as well as enhancing the aesthetic quality of the environ­
ment.  Management of the fishery will be applied to production of
muskellunge, a species which is well adapted to the characteristics of
the year-around pool and which is much sought after by sportsmen.  The
pool will inundate about 7,4 miles of natural stream and the associated
biotic community.  The environment adjacent to the pool will undergo
change because of the probable rise of the water table, modification
of the microclimate, and occasional inundation by flood waters.

On the land to be occupied by the recreation pool there are
a number of archaeological sites, and more sites are located within the
maximum flood control pool (elevation 660.3).  While the project may
result in the loss or decreased accessibility of some information obtain­
able by archaeological techniques, the archaeological and historic
sites of significance will be salvaged prior to filling the pool.
Dr. John Blank of Cleveland State University is conducting an archeologi­
cal study for the National Park Service to assure a proper salvage program.

Evaporation of water from the impoundment is expected to total
about 3,500 acre-feet per year, reducing the annual average flow by about
10 c.f.s. to 290 c.f.s.

Physical characteristics of the area are unfavorable to the
creation of a malaria hazard.  In general, the flood plains are well
drained and it is unlikely that breeding of anopheles mosquitoes would
be supported by ponding of water resulting from reservoir fluctuations.
Any ponding revealed during normal reservoir operations will be drained
to prevent mosquito breeding.

As a result of having been impounded, the water released will
differ in characteristics from the unimpounded stream water.  Effects
that may result from the project include reduced turbidity because of
low velocities and long detention times; reduced hardness caused by
algae production of carbon dioxide and subsequent precipitation of
calcium carbonate; reduced color and biochemical oxygen demand caused

[PDF page 7]
by long detention times, permitting biodegradation; reduced coliform
density caused by increased detention time, permitting natural die-off;
and equalizing action, smoothing high concentrations of any incoming
pollutants*  Other incidental effects that may occur when the water is
impounded include reduced velocities which may cause floating debris
to accumulate on the lake shoreline; lower reaeration caused by lower
velocities and increased depth; a backup of pollutants caused by a
changing water surface profile; increased algae problems appearing as
scums or taste and odor in the water, both caused by the increased
detention time in the reservoir; reduced bottom scour because of
increased depth; and thermal stratification, possibly resulting in the
accumulation of iron and manganese in the hypolimnion; production of
hydrogen sulfide, possibly lowering the pH of the water; and reduced
aerobic biodegradation.  The outlet structure will be designed with
multiple level intakes of adequate hydraulic capacity to permit control
of the strata from which water is discharged.  Intake levels will be
selected to provide discharges of good quality water.

The impoundment will cause deposition of much of the sediment
load of the stream in the reservoir, which will result in a progressive
change in the characteristics of the aquatic habitat and aggradation
of the stream immediately upstream from the reservoir.  Based upon
experience at similar reservoirs, it is estimated that the annual sedi­
mentation rate will average about 0.22 acre-foot per square mile of
controlled drainage.  A minimum pool will be provided in the reservoir
that will have adequate storage capacity to contain the anticipated
sedimentation without affecting storage for other project purposes
within the economic life of the reservoir.  Deposition of the sediment
in the reservoir will permit the discharge of relatively sediment-free
water.  This may result in degradation of the channel for a distance
downstream from the dam.  Channel degradation downstream from the proj­
ect and aggradation along the upstream reaches are expected to be
inconsequential.  The reduction of silt in the tailwater is expected
to improve the productivity of the fishery.

The impoundment and the associated lands ultimately will serve
an estimated 663,000 visitors per year, including about 59,000 fishermen
and hunters.  To accommodate and control these users, facilities such
as roads, boat launching ramps, rest rooms, campsites, and picnic areas
will be constructed.  In order to serve the recreationists efficiently
and to reserve other areas for wildlife, the recreational development
will be concentrated in several locations along the north side of the
reservoir.  A side effect of the concentration of people at the project
will be production of a large amount of sewage.  This sewage, which
will be given tertiary treatment, may lead to increases in nutrient
levels of the impounded and discharged water.

5.  Alternatives to the proposed action.  Alternatives to the proj­
ect that would help alleviate flood problems if applied either separately
or in combinations include the followings  Construction of concrete walls
or earth levees as barriers against floods; improvement of existing
channels to increase their carrying capacity by clearing, enlarging,
or straightening; diversion of flood waters from existing channels into
other existing or new channels; construction of retarding or detention
reservoirs on small and large tributaries to withhold flows in excess
of natural channel capacities; evacuation of overflow area; floodproof­
ing of improvements tliat are susceptible to flood damages; zoning of
areas to control further development on flood plains; and a system of
flood insurance to help protect occupants of the flood plain from damages
while discouraging further imprudent development of the flood plain.
Flood walls and/or levees would be economically infeasible alternatives
to the project because of the great length and the height which would
be required to afford protection, and would have a great and generally
adverse environmental impact on the river valley if used extensively.
Channel modifications to improve hydraulic characteristics so as to con­
vey floodwater more rapidly would involve a massive disruption of the
river and riverbanks.  Diversionary floodways would affect large amounts
of level land in the region.  Retarding or detention reservoirs on tribu­
taries could help reduce flood heights locally, but to be as effective
as the Salt Creek Lake project in reducing flood heights on Salt Creek
and the Scioto and Ohio Rivers, a great nunber of small projects to
control the runoff from an equivalent drainage area would be required.
Evacuation of residents and industries from areas subject to flooding
would be disruptive socially and would leave considerable potential for
flood damage to roads, railroads, and crops.  The combination of flood
walls and/or levees around relatively concentrated developments and the
evacuation of dispersed developments could avoid some of the problems
associated with the alternatives when applied separately.  Floodproof­
ing of improvements, while infeasible for all structures in all locations,
might be used in combination with local protection works and evacuation
of the flood plain so as to minimize flood damages and disturbance of

[PDF page 11]
the natural and cultural environment.  Floodproofing would not avoid
many problems of health and safety associated with flooding.  Zoning
could help to prevent future damages with little adverse environmental
effect but would require implementation by State and local governments.
Flood insurance could similarly discourage further imprudent develop­
ment of the flood plain and alleviate economic hardship to present
occupants of the flood plain.  If no action is taken to control flood
damages and associated problems, they will continue to occur and to
increase.

Alternatives to the project that would result in increased
recreational use or in increased quality of use include the provision
of public access areas and recreational facilities along parts of the
stream, implementation of a program of fishery management in the stream
and wildlife management in the area, and an increase in recreational
development on other proposed and existing reservoirs in the region.
Public recreation areas along the stream, while avoiding many of the
adverse effects of the reservoir project, probably would accomimdate
fewer visitors.  Intensified development at other recreatiou areas in
the region would be an alternative if this could be done without over­
crowding, but the areas with broad-water are already used very heavily.
If no action is taken to increase opportunities for outdoor recreation,
the existing shortage will be aggravated.

Any one of the several purposes to be served by the Salt
Creek Lake could be satisfied by a single-purpose alternative or by
a combination of alternative means.  A series or combination of
alternative measures designed  to serve all facets of water resource
management as effectively as the authorized project would result in
a complex program requiring decisive and coordinated action at the
Federal, State, and local levels of government, would be less feasible
economically, and would have environmental impact that may be similar
to that of the multiple-purpose project.

COMMENTS CONCERNING AN ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT
ON THE PROPOSED SALT CREEK RESERVOIR,
SALT CREEK, SCIOTO RIVER BASIN, OHIO

by

Carol B. Stain
The Ohio State University
Museum of Zoology

The proposed Salt Creek Reservoir project, as proposed by the U. S. Army Corps
of Engineers, would consist of a dam and other facilities on Salt Creek, a tributary
of the Scioto River, in Ross County, Ohio.  The dam, to be located 10.8 miles above
the mouth of Salt Creek, will convert the Salt Creek valley into a lake from Ross
County through Vinton County and extending into Hocking County.

The two reasons for the construction of this dam are "flood control, recreation,
and fish and wildlife enhancement, with Incidental redevelopment benefits," accord­
ing to the Environmental Statement prepared by the U. S. Army Engineers.  Yet it is
also noted in the Statement (page 2) that "Salt Creek supports good to excellent pop­
ulations of muskellunge, channel catfish, shovelhead catfish, smallmouth bass,
spotted bass, rock bass, sunfish, and rough fish.  Stream fishing is cf importance in
this ssction of Ohio... Average annual fisherman-use on Salt Creek within and down­
stream from the project area is about 960 man-days of fishing per mile."  It is also
claimed that "frequent natural low flows detract from the productivity of the fish­
ery and from the aesthetic appeal of the stream."

The many fine species of game fish and the great variety of other stream organ­
isms which survive today in Salt Creek exist there because they have evolved for
millions of years in the free-flowing stream habitats of the Appalachian Plateau
region.  They are eminently suited for survival in these undammed streams with their
wide variation in flow because those individuals which possessed the abilities and
characteristics necessary to survive during periods of low flow and high flow have
survived and have passed these characteristics on to their descendants.  Their con­
tinued existence may well depend upon fluctuation in stream flow.  These animals
are successful today in Salt Creek because this stream still retains the essential
Characteristics of the environment in which they evolved.  Its flow varies naturally
with the seasons.  Its current is swift, and the water is highly oxygenated and not
severely polluted.  There is a wide variety of habitat niches, enabling a wide vari­
ety of species to survive in the alternating riffles, runs, and pools of Salt Creek.

All of this variety provides an immensely interesting recreational experience
for the fisherman who walks the stream simply to see what is around the next bend.
He can often predict what kind of fish he is likely to catch in a particular pool or
riffle if he uses a certain type of tackle, from worm and bent pin to sophisticated
fly rod.

If Salt Creek is impounded and its periods of high and low flow are eliminated,
the natural habitat will be drastically altered within and downstream from the proj­
ect area.  It is claimed (page 3) that this regulation of flow

"will prevent periods of extreme low flow such as occur under
normal (unregulated) conditions and thus will increase the
capacity of the stream to assimilate pollutants.  This also
will increase the capacity of the stream to support aquatic
life and riparian vegetation, and will maintain the typical
character of the stream by preventing its 'going dry' in the
fall."

[PDF page 54]
This statement is evidently contradictory.  If periods of low flow occur during na­
tural (unregulated) conditions, then they are typical of the stream.

Use of the reservoir as a toilet tank to flush sewage and other pollutants down
the stream during dry periods may Indeed dilute the pollutants enough to cause less
damage to the aquatic biota.  But is this going to "maintain the typical character
of the stream"?  Would it not be better to adequately treat the pollutants instead
of flushing them downstream to Hlgby, Waverly, Piketon, Lucasville, and the Ohio
River cities?

No evidence is presented in support of the claim that the regulation of flow
"will increase the capacity of the stream to support aquatic life and riparian veget­
ation."  Nor does the report explain which types of aquatic^ Jifa and riparian vegeta­
tion will be benefited.  In fact, the only forms of life which are mentioned in the
report are man and the game birds, mammals, and fish!  No mention is made of the many
species of trees, flowering plants, and ferns which draw hundreds of students, photog­
raphers, and amateur botanists to this section of the Appalachian Plateau every year.
The songbirds which are the delight of many hikers and ornithologists from Ohio and
neighboring states are virtually ignored.  The variety of insects and other small
but fascinating and valuable members of the Salt Creek valley ecosystem are not even
considered.  The frogs, turtles, salamanders, snails, crayfish, clams, and other
kinds of animals which inhabit Salt Creek have not even been inventoried.  There has
been no study which will predict the probable effects of the proposed project on thesi
plants and animals.

Perhaps these "lesser" plants and animals have been ignored in studies such as
this one because no man must buy a license to gather wild mushrooms, to photograph
a warbler on its nest, to collect the delicate and intricately patterned mollusk
shells, or simply to listen to the music of a free-flowing stream rushing over a
bouldery riffle.  Yet the human species is richer for these things, and millions of
people yearly desert the industrial urban centers to enjoy such simple pleasures in
the few relatively "natural" areas which remain in America.  Ohio has far fewer of
these precious areas than many other states.  Must her citizens be denied yet another
one in order to provide more industrial sites for more potentially polluting in­
dustries?  It would seem that, as concerned citizens of this state, we should be con­
cerned with preserving the quality of life in Ohio, not merely with the number of
people who can be packed within its borders.  The more people there are, the more
wild areas will be needed to relieve the urban stresses of the cities.  Let us take
care lest we turn the beautiful Salt Creek valley into a glorified farm pond.

f  t
The wide variety of plants which survive in the valley today provide the variety
of food types and habitat niches for the many kinds of animals.  The smaller animals,
usually ignored by the average sportsman, nevertheless are vital members in the web
of life which supports the fish and game which he hunts.  If the proposed dam is
built, most of the variety of aquatic life in the valley will be eliminated.  Only
a very few of our native species are adapted to survive in lakes.  Elimination of
periods of very low and very high floods below the dam will inevitably destroy part
of the natural environment below the dam.  The water temperature of the stream will
certainly be altered, affecting the breeding behavior and other parts of the life
cycles of the animals of the stream both above and below the dam.  For example, the
muskellunge, which occurs naturally in Salt Creek today, has been introduced into
many artificial impoundments across Ohio.  Even though the stocked individuals may
survive in some of these reservoirs, none have been known to succeed in reproducing
in any of Ohio's artificial lakes.  The spring floods, which normally spread a layer
of fertile silt over the floodplain of the stream, making it a rich soil for agri­
cultural crops and native floodplain vegetation, will be eliminated.  They will no
longer sweep the channel of the stream free of silt, maintaining crevices between the
rocks and gravel of the stream bed available for the insects, crayfish, and sala­
manders to live and grow.  If these retreats are silted up because of the constant

[PDF page 55]
flow, then these animals will be eliminated.  If they are eliminated, what will pro­
vide food for tha "good to excellent populations of muskellunge, channel catfish,
shovelhead catfish, smallmouth bass, spotted bass, rock bass, sunfish, and rough
fish" which inhabit Salt Creek today?  Where, for that matter, will these fish find
the varied kinds of habitat they need for shalter?

It would seem to be not only advisable, but essential that a detailed survey of
all of the kinds of organisms which now inhabit the Salt Creek valley ecosystem
should be made.  A team of competent botanists, zoologists, and other natural scien­
tists should certainly be employed to study the present biota of the area and the
interdependencies of the various species, and to evaluate the probable impact of the
project on each of these species.  Then, and only then, can a reasonably accurate
prediction of the environmental impact of the proposed project be made.

The Environmental Statement notes (page 4) that "archaeological sites of sig­
nificance will be salvaged prior to filling the pool."  However, the Statement does
not take note of the extensive natural history sites and rare species which occur
within the project area; nor does it state that any of these will be "salvaged" prior
to the construction of the dam or the filling of the pool.  This is a serious omis­
sion.  Samples of the aquatic and terrestrial plants and animals which occupy Salt
Creek and its floodplain area should certainly be collected and carefully preserved in
established research museum collections before they and their habitat are irreversibly
and irretrievably destroyed by the construction of this dam.  These specimens,
properly documented, would be of inestimable value in evaluating the actual environ­
mental impact of the project, if the project is completed.  They will help biologists
of future generations to know something of the native fauna and flora of Ohio in an
area which will by then have been destroyed.

These specimens will also be extremely valuable in predicting the probable en­
vironmental impact of projects such as this one which may be proposed in the future.
It is essential that we be able to foresee at least the most important of the many
subtle and often intricate long-term effects of our changing the environment in
which we live before we make changes which may result in making this planet uninhab­
itable for future generations of mankind.  Only by carefully studying the actual ef­
fects of future engineering schemes.

Any evaluation of the environmental impact of the project depends upon the scale
of values assigned by the evaluators.  Assigning the U. S. Army Corps of Engineers to
evaluate the probable impact of the project which they are to build is not unlike
asking a beaver to evaluate the impact of a beaver dam, or a hungry child to object­
ively evaluate the benefit-to-cost ratio of an ice cream cone.  If the best interests
of £he whole population are to be served, the probable effects of the construction
of such a project must be studied in advance by competent but objective specialists
who represent all of the people who will be affected in the long run by the project.
They will be more likely to present an unbiased opinion if their jobs or contracts
do not depend on their ability to demonstrate that the benefits will exceed the costs
to the taxpayers and the environment.  Just as the best interests of the public are
served if concerned, objective biologists and health authorities set the standards of

the;..  residents of Vinton County.  Are the loss of these productive farms and the
tax revenue they generate,  the loss of the biologically rich stream with, its scenic
qualities, its natural recreation potential, and its noted fishery,  truly less im-
portant in the long run than a few extfa jobs and additional acres of water surface
for recreation?  Is the potential flood protection the project would give the down­
stream communities truly of greater importance than the damage which would be caused
by permanently flooding the rich Vinton County farmland?

As the Environmental Statement notes, there are a number of possible alterna­
tive ways to achieve flood control and develop the recreation potential of Salt
Creek without building the proposed dam.  Most of these alternatives would provide
less revenue to the Corps of Engineers and their contracting firms, but they would
save the American taxpayer great sums of money, and some of them undoubtedly would
have better long-range environmental effects.

The zoning of low-lying areas to control further development on flood plains
certainly seems to be a very sensible and promising alternative to impoundment of the
stream.  If the floodplain land were zoned as open space for agricultural and recre­
ational uses, the highland sites couldbereserved for woodlands, homes, industries,
and other structures.  If this were done, then the rivers of our country could be
allowed to run free, with their valuable fisheries and their aesthetic values largely
unimpaired by unwise development and pollution.  The taxpayers would pay far less for
flood control projects, since they would not be needed.  Homeowners on the uplands
could enjoy the aesthetic values of open space and wild lands near their homes.  The
enormous economic damage and loss of life which now occur when a major river over­
flows its banks would be far less if flood plains were zoned for use only by such
structures and activities as would not be harmed by periodic flooding.

As the Environmental Statement notes, "Alternatives to the project that would
result in increased recreational use or in increased quality of use include the pro­
vision of public access areas and recreational facilities along parts of the stream,
implementation of a program of fishery management in the stream and wildlife manage­
ment in the area, and an increase in the recreational development in nearby State
and National forests."  Such alternatives, combined with proper floodplain zoning,
could very likely achieve all of the benefits of the proposed dam, as well as make
a far more stable and long-lasting step toward a high quality environment for all
mankind— and at far less cost to the taxpayer than the proposed dam.

Such alternatives should be given careful and objective consideration by a con­
cerned jury representative of the people.  They should recognize that a dam would be
a costly and strictly temporary solution to the problem of flooding, since, as even
the Corps of Engineers admits (page 8)

"The project was formulated on the basis of having an economic
life of 100 years.  The physical life of the project will likely
be considerably in excess of that period.  Major rehabilitation
or reallocation cf storages may be required upon expiration of
the project life."

However, a thoughtful program of flood-plain zoning and development of recreational
resources, carried out gradually at little expense over the next hundred years,
could provide the benefits of a beautiful and relatively unaltered natural environ­
ment, largely undamaged by periodic flooding, as a heritage for our great-great
grandchildren.  Will they not appreciate this far more than a weedy mudflat behind an
ancient wall, with crowded industrial cities huddled behind other walls along the
rivers far downstream?  The choice is ours.

Columbus, Ohio
12 February 1971

SALT CREEK LAKE

1.  Project description.  The Salt Creek Lake project will con­
sist of the construction and operation of a dam and other facilities
for flood control, recreation, and fish and wildlife enhancement, with
incidental redevelopment benefits.  The Salt Creek Lake is one unit in
the comprehensive plan for water resources development of the Scioto
River Basin.  The plan consists of seven major reservoir projects
(two are operational, two under construction, and the other three in
planning and design), one local protection project,  and one channel
improvement project.  Project formulation and system analysis are dis­
cussed in House Document No.  587 of the 87th Congress, 2nd Session.
The dam is to be located in Ross County, Ohio, on Salt Creek, 10.8
miles above its confluence with Scioto River.  It will regulate the
runoff from a 285 square mile watershed.  As presently planned, the
pool to be maintained will be at elevation 625.0 feet above mean sea
level, will have a surface area of about 1,233 acres, and a shoreline
length of about 23 miles;  storage capacity of 94,002 acre-feet will be
available for temporary impoundment of water during flood periods.
The larger part of the reservoir will be in Vinton County, but it will
extend into Hocking County.  The project, authorized by the Flood Con­
trol Act of 1962, currently Is in the advanced engineering and design
stage.  Its benefit-to-cost ratio is 1.15 to 1.

2.  Environmental setting without the project.  The Salt Creek
Lake project site is in the Appalachian Region, and in the vicinity
many of the social and economic problems typical of Appalachia are
evident.  Ross County (which is on the periphery of Appalachia and
straddles the Scioto River valley, with its attendant transportation,
industry, and agriculture)  is one of the richest counties in Appalachian
Ohio.  On the other hand, Vinton County, which contains the major por­
tion of the area to be acquired for the project,  is one of the more
depressed counties in Ohio.  In both counties, however, in comparison
with the State as a whole and with the Nation, the'population is rela­
tively sparse and is declining, the level of education is low, family
income is low, housing conditions are poor, and per capita property
taxes are low.  Nevertheless, in June 1970, unemployment was 4.0 per­
cent in Ross County and 4.3 percent in Vinton County, these rates being
close to the average for State and Nation.

The reservoir site is in the unglaciated Kanawha Section of
the Appalachian Plateau physiographic province, an area of maturely
dissected topography.  Total relief in the project area is about 500
feet, and the hillsides are frequently steep.  In the project area,
Salt Creek has formed a relativelv broad, alluvial plain, averaging
about half a mile wide.  The cleared and cultivated areas of the farms
occupy the valley floors and extend up over the toes of the hills.
The tipper slopes are densely forested.

[PDF page 4]
Salt Creek heads in a ground moraine within the southeastern
edge of the glaciated portion of central Ohio.  From there it flows
generally southward through relatively level, glaciated terrain, then
turns southwest and flows in a deeply entrenched valley through rugged,
unglaciated terrain to its confluence with the Scioto, downriver from
Chillicothe.  The stream gradient averages about 10 feet to the mile.
In the project reach, Salt Creek is underlain by as much as 80 feet of
alluvium, as it traverses a series of silted pools interrupted by sand,
gravel, and rubble riffles.

The average annual flow of Salt Creek at the dam site is 300
cubic feet per second, varying from a March normal average of 738 c.f.s.
to an October normal average of 26 c.f.s.  Minimum average flow for a
month has dropped below 8 c.f.s. and instantaneous low flows have been
recorded at less than 5 c.f.s., while brief flood flow has exceeded
34,000 c.f.s.

Flood flows from Salt Creek contribute to the damage of
several towns along the Scioto River (Higby, Waverly, Piketon, and
Lucasville) and to towns and industries along the Ohio River.  Recurring
flooding along the reach of Salt Creek downstream from the project makes
the land there undesirable for industrial development, notwithstanding
that it is level, and well served by highways and railroads.

Frequent natural low flows restrict assimilative capacity
thereby affecting productivity of the fishery and the aesthetic appeal
of the stream.

Salt Creek in its present condition supports good to excellent
populations of muskellunge, channel catfish,  shovelhead catfish, small-
mouth bass, spotted bass, rock bass, sunfish, and rough fish.  Stream
fishing is of importance in this section of Ohio, as practically no
reservoir fishing is available.  Private owners of lands adjoining the
project reach of Salt Creek permit public use of the stream, which re­
sults in heavy fishing pressure.  Average annual fisherman-use on Salt
Creek within and downstream from the project area is about 960 man-days
of fishing per mile.

Salt Creek has waterfowl resource value in providing good duck
nesting and resting areas.  Black and mallard ducks use the area occa­
sionally.  Hunter use is estimated at the average annual rate of one
hunter-day per mile of stream.  Fair populations of muskrat and mink
occur along Salt Creek.

The valley floor is largely farm-game habitat, supporting
primarily rabbits, quail, raccoon, and songbirds.  In the forested hills
white-tailed deer, fox, gray squirrels, ruffed grouse, and turkey are
present.  Fox hunting and raccoon hunting with dogs are popular sports.
Average annual hunting use is estimated at 112 man-days per square mile.

3.  The environmental impact of the proposed action.  The proposed
project will provide water storage which will be used for flood control,
general recreation, and fish and wildlife recreation.  Along with the
effects resulting directly from these major intended purposes,  there
will be nunerous effects on the environment resulting from the processes
initiated by the project.

The amount of water released from the dam will be regulated
so as to decrease peak flow.  This will alleviate the recurring, destruc­
tive floods along the Scioto River and contribute to the reduction of
flooding on the Ohio River.  Monetary savings attributable to flood
reduction are expected to average $740,000 annually.  Intangible effects
will include reduced possibility of death,  injury, or illness resulting
from floods; reduction of the social and economic insecurity caused by
frequent flooding; lessening of the necessity to commit labor and mate­
rial to emergency and relief operations; and reduced aesthetic degrada­
tion of communities subject to floods.  Incidental effects of flood re­
duction include a decrease  in the competence of the stream to transport
larger particles, possibly resulting in a change in the hydraulic and
biologic characteristics of the riverbed.

The flood protection resulting from the project will increase
the attractiveness of the land downstream and will change existing land-
use patterns.  The land will probably be converted to a higher economic
use, with mare residences and mare businesses.  Several parcels of land
near Londonderry presently have limited potential for industrial and
commercial use.  Existence of the reservoir will, however, foster the
growth of the community, and the economic potential of the land will
be increased by reason of reservoir-related activities.

The dam will regulate the base flow of the stream so that from
April through November it does not drop below 20 c.f.s., and for the
remainder of the year below 10 c.f.s.  This regulation will prevent
periods of extreme low flow such as occur under normal (unregulated)
conditions and thus will increase the ability of the stream (and the
Scioto River) to assimilate pollutants.  In addition to treated and
industrial and municipal wastes, pollutants enter the streams from
normal bank erosion and from runoff or drainage from agricultural lands
and developed areas thereby involving such contaminents as sediment,
fertilizers, pesticides, herbicides, and chemicals or salts used for
ice and snow control.  Augmentation of low flows also will increase the
capacity of the stream to support some types of aquatic life and riparian
vegetation, will maintain the visual character of the stream by prevent­
ing its "going dry"  in the fall, and will help maintain water quality
standards along the lower reaches of the Scioto River.

[PDF page 6]
A 1,233-acre recreation pool with a capacity of 11,462 acre-
feet will be maintained at elevation 625 throughout the year except
when detained flood waters raise the level or when, on rare occasions,
the minimum release exceeds the inflow and the level is lowered.  The
pool will be relatively stable and, therefore,  is expected to develop
an ecosystem similar to that of a natural lake.  Reservoir clearing
will be coordinated with state officials to facilitate fish and wildlife
management.  The lake will provide permanent habitat for water-associated
mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and birds, as well as fish.  The U. S.
Fish and Wildlife Service indicates that the,relative stability of the
pool will be conducive to the establishment of permanent populations
of life forms that will increase the opportunity to enjoy non-consumptive
use of wildlife as well as enhancing the aesthetic quality of the environ­
ment.  Management of the fishery will be applied to production of
muskellunge, a species which is well adapted to the characteristics of
the year-around pool and which is much sought after by sportsmen.  The
pool will inundate about 7,4 miles of natural stream and the associated
biotic community.  The environment adjacent to the pool will undergo
change because of the probable rise of the water table, modification
of the microclimate, and occasional inundation by flood waters.

On the land to be occupied by the recreation pool there are
a number of archaeological sites, and more sites are located within the
maximum flood control pool (elevation 660.3).  While the project may
result in the loss or decreased accessibility of some information obtain­
able by archaeological techniques, the archaeological and historic
sites of significance will be salvaged prior to filling the pool.
Dr. John Blank of Cleveland State University is conducting an archeologi­
cal study for the National Park Service to assure a proper salvage program.

Evaporation of water from the impoundment is expected to total
about 3,500 acre-feet per year, reducing the annual average flow by about
10 c.f.s. to 290 c.f.s.

Physical characteristics of the area are unfavorable to the
creation of a malaria hazard.  In general, the flood plains are well
drained and it is unlikely that breeding of anopheles mosquitoes would
be supported by ponding of water resulting from reservoir fluctuations.
Any ponding revealed during normal reservoir operations will be drained
to prevent mosquito breeding.

As a result of having been impounded, the water released will
differ in characteristics from the unimpounded stream water.  Effects
that may result from the project include reduced turbidity because of
low velocities and long detention times; reduced hardness caused by
algae production of carbon dioxide and subsequent precipitation of
calcium carbonate; reduced color and biochemical oxygen demand caused

[PDF page 7]
by long detention times, permitting biodegradation; reduced coliform
density caused by increased detention time, permitting natural die-off;
and equalizing action, smoothing high concentrations of any incoming
pollutants*  Other incidental effects that may occur when the water is
impounded include reduced velocities which may cause floating debris
to accumulate on the lake shoreline; lower reaeration caused by lower
velocities and increased depth; a backup of pollutants caused by a
changing water surface profile; increased algae problems appearing as
scums or taste and odor in the water, both caused by the increased
detention time in the reservoir; reduced bottom scour because of
increased depth; and thermal stratification, possibly resulting in the
accumulation of iron and manganese in the hypolimnion; production of
hydrogen sulfide, possibly lowering the pH of the water; and reduced
aerobic biodegradation.  The outlet structure will be designed with
multiple level intakes of adequate hydraulic capacity to permit control
of the strata from which water is discharged.  Intake levels will be
selected to provide discharges of good quality water.

The impoundment will cause deposition of much of the sediment
load of the stream in the reservoir, which will result in a progressive
change in the characteristics of the aquatic habitat and aggradation
of the stream immediately upstream from the reservoir.  Based upon
experience at similar reservoirs, it is estimated that the annual sedi­
mentation rate will average about 0.22 acre-foot per square mile of
controlled drainage.  A minimum pool will be provided in the reservoir
that will have adequate storage capacity to contain the anticipated
sedimentation without affecting storage for other project purposes
within the economic life of the reservoir.  Deposition of the sediment
in the reservoir will permit the discharge of relatively sediment-free
water.  This may result in degradation of the channel for a distance
downstream from the dam.  Channel degradation downstream from the proj­
ect and aggradation along the upstream reaches are expected to be
inconsequential.  The reduction of silt in the tailwater is expected
to improve the productivity of the fishery.

The impoundment and the associated lands ultimately will serve
an estimated 663,000 visitors per year, including about 59,000 fishermen
and hunters.  To accommodate and control these users, facilities such
as roads, boat launching ramps, rest rooms, campsites, and picnic areas
will be constructed.  In order to serve the recreationists efficiently
and to reserve other areas for wildlife, the recreational development
will be concentrated in several locations along the north side of the
reservoir.  A side effect of the concentration of people at the project
will be production of a large amount of sewage.  This sewage, which
will be given tertiary treatment, may lead to increases in nutrient
levels of the impounded and discharged water.

[PDF page 8]
A more telling effect of the development of the recreational
resource will be the creation of about 100 additional jobs in the serv­
ice sector of the regional economy.  Another boost to the economy will
come from the employment of an estimated 185 workers for construction
of the project, over a period of four years, and their annual payroll
of $1.*+ million.

The building of the project will result in accelerated erosion
of parts of the project lands and in an increased sediment load in the
stream.  These temporary effects will be minimized by controlled con­
struction practices.  Disturbed areas will be seeded or otherwise treated
to avoid erosion as well as for aesthetic purposes.  The construction

Acquisition of land for the project and the consequent removal
of the residents will change some communal and familial patterns of the
individuals involved.  About 70 persons now live on the land which will
be acquired.  The community of Eagle Mills, which consists of about
10 residential properties, will cease to exist.  Land use also will
change.  Acquisition of land necessary for  the project will involve

There are no known mineral resources on the project lands

The construction and operation of the reservoir is expected
to strengthen the fiscal position of local governments and school dis­
tricts, despite the loss of property tax base and the increased demand
for governmental services by newly attracted residents and tourists.
Studies of other reservoirs have shown that the property tax base in­
creases more rapidly in counties containing a reservoir than in other
counties,  and, further, that the initial loss in the tax base caused
by removal of land from the tax rolls tends to be recovered in time
through more rapid expansion.  In addition,  school districts losing
more than 10 percent of their tax base to Federal projects can be
aided by a subsidy.

5.  Alternatives to the proposed action.  Alternatives to the proj­
ect that would help alleviate flood problems if applied either separately
or in combinations include the followings  Construction of concrete walls
or earth levees as barriers against floods; improvement of existing
channels to increase their carrying capacity by clearing, enlarging,
or straightening; diversion of flood waters from existing channels into
other existing or new channels; construction of retarding or detention
reservoirs on small and large tributaries to withhold flows in excess
of natural channel capacities; evacuation of overflow area; floodproof­
ing of improvements tliat are susceptible to flood damages; zoning of
areas to control further development on flood plains; and a system of
flood insurance to help protect occupants of the flood plain from damages
while discouraging further imprudent development of the flood plain.
Flood walls and/or levees would be economically infeasible alternatives
to the project because of the great length and the height which would
be required to afford protection, and would have a great and generally
adverse environmental impact on the river valley if used extensively.
Channel modifications to improve hydraulic characteristics so as to con­
vey floodwater more rapidly would involve a massive disruption of the
river and riverbanks.  Diversionary floodways would affect large amounts
of level land in the region.  Retarding or detention reservoirs on tribu­
taries could help reduce flood heights locally, but to be as effective
as the Salt Creek Lake project in reducing flood heights on Salt Creek
and the Scioto and Ohio Rivers, a great nunber of small projects to
control the runoff from an equivalent drainage area would be required.
Evacuation of residents and industries from areas subject to flooding
would be disruptive socially and would leave considerable potential for
flood damage to roads, railroads, and crops.  The combination of flood
walls and/or levees around relatively concentrated developments and the
evacuation of dispersed developments could avoid some of the problems
associated with the alternatives when applied separately.  Floodproof­
ing of improvements, while infeasible for all structures in all locations,
might be used in combination with local protection works and evacuation
of the flood plain so as to minimize flood damages and disturbance of

[PDF page 11]
the natural and cultural environment.  Floodproofing would not avoid
many problems of health and safety associated with flooding.  Zoning
could help to prevent future damages with little adverse environmental
effect but would require implementation by State and local governments.
Flood insurance could similarly discourage further imprudent develop­
ment of the flood plain and alleviate economic hardship to present
occupants of the flood plain.  If no action is taken to control flood
damages and associated problems, they will continue to occur and to
increase.

Alternatives to the project that would result in increased
recreational use or in increased quality of use include the provision
of public access areas and recreational facilities along parts of the
stream, implementation of a program of fishery management in the stream
and wildlife management in the area, and an increase in recreational
development on other proposed and existing reservoirs in the region.
Public recreation areas along the stream, while avoiding many of the
adverse effects of the reservoir project, probably would accomimdate
fewer visitors.  Intensified development at other recreatiou areas in
the region would be an alternative if this could be done without over­
crowding, but the areas with broad-water are already used very heavily.
If no action is taken to increase opportunities for outdoor recreation,
the existing shortage will be aggravated.

Any one of the several purposes to be served by the Salt
Creek Lake could be satisfied by a single-purpose alternative or by
a combination of alternative means.  A series or combination of
alternative measures designed  to serve all facets of water resource
management as effectively as the authorized project would result in
a complex program requiring decisive and coordinated action at the
Federal, State, and local levels of government, would be less feasible
economically, and would have environmental impact that may be similar
to that of the multiple-purpose project.

On the project lands many of the present uses of the environment will

streams within the project area will be abandoned or relocated as appro­

ruption of people and communities downstream, by increasing usability

stream, by creating a major recreational resource, and by contributing

to economic development.  The project was formulated on the basis of

Our comments are presented under the headings of your draft environmental
statement and are based upon information on hand in our regional office and

Although this section is adequate, it would be helpful if information on
pool elevations and other reservoir data were also presented.

attitudes.  Improving the methods of preventing and treating pollutants

treatment measures are developed, low-flow augmentation is a means

preservation of undeveloped portions by preventing unrestricted industrial,

COMMENTS CONCERNING AN ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT
ON THE PROPOSED SALT CREEK RESERVOIR,
SALT CREEK, SCIOTO RIVER BASIN, OHIO

by

Carol B. Stain
The Ohio State University
Museum of Zoology

The proposed Salt Creek Reservoir project, as proposed by the U. S. Army Corps
of Engineers, would consist of a dam and other facilities on Salt Creek, a tributary
of the Scioto River, in Ross County, Ohio.  The dam, to be located 10.8 miles above
the mouth of Salt Creek, will convert the Salt Creek valley into a lake from Ross
County through Vinton County and extending into Hocking County.

The two reasons for the construction of this dam are "flood control, recreation,
and fish and wildlife enhancement, with Incidental redevelopment benefits," accord­
ing to the Environmental Statement prepared by the U. S. Army Engineers.  Yet it is
also noted in the Statement (page 2) that "Salt Creek supports good to excellent pop­
ulations of muskellunge, channel catfish, shovelhead catfish, smallmouth bass,
spotted bass, rock bass, sunfish, and rough fish.  Stream fishing is cf importance in
this ssction of Ohio... Average annual fisherman-use on Salt Creek within and down­
stream from the project area is about 960 man-days of fishing per mile."  It is also
claimed that "frequent natural low flows detract from the productivity of the fish­
ery and from the aesthetic appeal of the stream."

The many fine species of game fish and the great variety of other stream organ­
isms which survive today in Salt Creek exist there because they have evolved for
millions of years in the free-flowing stream habitats of the Appalachian Plateau
region.  They are eminently suited for survival in these undammed streams with their
wide variation in flow because those individuals which possessed the abilities and
characteristics necessary to survive during periods of low flow and high flow have
survived and have passed these characteristics on to their descendants.  Their con­
tinued existence may well depend upon fluctuation in stream flow.  These animals
are successful today in Salt Creek because this stream still retains the essential
Characteristics of the environment in which they evolved.  Its flow varies naturally
with the seasons.  Its current is swift, and the water is highly oxygenated and not
severely polluted.  There is a wide variety of habitat niches, enabling a wide vari­
ety of species to survive in the alternating riffles, runs, and pools of Salt Creek.

All of this variety provides an immensely interesting recreational experience
for the fisherman who walks the stream simply to see what is around the next bend.
He can often predict what kind of fish he is likely to catch in a particular pool or
riffle if he uses a certain type of tackle, from worm and bent pin to sophisticated
fly rod.

If Salt Creek is impounded and its periods of high and low flow are eliminated,
the natural habitat will be drastically altered within and downstream from the proj­
ect area.  It is claimed (page 3) that this regulation of flow

"will prevent periods of extreme low flow such as occur under
normal (unregulated) conditions and thus will increase the
capacity of the stream to assimilate pollutants.  This also
will increase the capacity of the stream to support aquatic
life and riparian vegetation, and will maintain the typical
character of the stream by preventing its 'going dry' in the
fall."

[PDF page 54]
This statement is evidently contradictory.  If periods of low flow occur during na­
tural (unregulated) conditions, then they are typical of the stream.

Use of the reservoir as a toilet tank to flush sewage and other pollutants down
the stream during dry periods may Indeed dilute the pollutants enough to cause less
damage to the aquatic biota.  But is this going to "maintain the typical character
of the stream"?  Would it not be better to adequately treat the pollutants instead
of flushing them downstream to Hlgby, Waverly, Piketon, Lucasville, and the Ohio
River cities?

No evidence is presented in support of the claim that the regulation of flow
"will increase the capacity of the stream to support aquatic life and riparian veget­
ation."  Nor does the report explain which types of aquatic^ Jifa and riparian vegeta­
tion will be benefited.  In fact, the only forms of life which are mentioned in the
report are man and the game birds, mammals, and fish!  No mention is made of the many
species of trees, flowering plants, and ferns which draw hundreds of students, photog­
raphers, and amateur botanists to this section of the Appalachian Plateau every year.
The songbirds which are the delight of many hikers and ornithologists from Ohio and
neighboring states are virtually ignored.  The variety of insects and other small
but fascinating and valuable members of the Salt Creek valley ecosystem are not even
considered.  The frogs, turtles, salamanders, snails, crayfish, clams, and other
kinds of animals which inhabit Salt Creek have not even been inventoried.  There has
been no study which will predict the probable effects of the proposed project on thesi
plants and animals.

Perhaps these "lesser" plants and animals have been ignored in studies such as
this one because no man must buy a license to gather wild mushrooms, to photograph
a warbler on its nest, to collect the delicate and intricately patterned mollusk
shells, or simply to listen to the music of a free-flowing stream rushing over a
bouldery riffle.  Yet the human species is richer for these things, and millions of
people yearly desert the industrial urban centers to enjoy such simple pleasures in
the few relatively "natural" areas which remain in America.  Ohio has far fewer of
these precious areas than many other states.  Must her citizens be denied yet another
one in order to provide more industrial sites for more potentially polluting in­
dustries?  It would seem that, as concerned citizens of this state, we should be con­
cerned with preserving the quality of life in Ohio, not merely with the number of
people who can be packed within its borders.  The more people there are, the more
wild areas will be needed to relieve the urban stresses of the cities.  Let us take
care lest we turn the beautiful Salt Creek valley into a glorified farm pond.

f  t
The wide variety of plants which survive in the valley today provide the variety
of food types and habitat niches for the many kinds of animals.  The smaller animals,
usually ignored by the average sportsman, nevertheless are vital members in the web
of life which supports the fish and game which he hunts.  If the proposed dam is
built, most of the variety of aquatic life in the valley will be eliminated.  Only
a very few of our native species are adapted to survive in lakes.  Elimination of
periods of very low and very high floods below the dam will inevitably destroy part
of the natural environment below the dam.  The water temperature of the stream will
certainly be altered, affecting the breeding behavior and other parts of the life
cycles of the animals of the stream both above and below the dam.  For example, the
muskellunge, which occurs naturally in Salt Creek today, has been introduced into
many artificial impoundments across Ohio.  Even though the stocked individuals may
survive in some of these reservoirs, none have been known to succeed in reproducing
in any of Ohio's artificial lakes.  The spring floods, which normally spread a layer
of fertile silt over the floodplain of the stream, making it a rich soil for agri­
cultural crops and native floodplain vegetation, will be eliminated.  They will no
longer sweep the channel of the stream free of silt, maintaining crevices between the
rocks and gravel of the stream bed available for the insects, crayfish, and sala­
manders to live and grow.  If these retreats are silted up because of the constant

[PDF page 55]
flow, then these animals will be eliminated.  If they are eliminated, what will pro­
vide food for tha "good to excellent populations of muskellunge, channel catfish,
shovelhead catfish, smallmouth bass, spotted bass, rock bass, sunfish, and rough
fish" which inhabit Salt Creek today?  Where, for that matter, will these fish find
the varied kinds of habitat they need for shalter?

It would seem to be not only advisable, but essential that a detailed survey of
all of the kinds of organisms which now inhabit the Salt Creek valley ecosystem
should be made.  A team of competent botanists, zoologists, and other natural scien­
tists should certainly be employed to study the present biota of the area and the
interdependencies of the various species, and to evaluate the probable impact of the
project on each of these species.  Then, and only then, can a reasonably accurate
prediction of the environmental impact of the proposed project be made.

The Environmental Statement notes (page 4) that "archaeological sites of sig­
nificance will be salvaged prior to filling the pool."  However, the Statement does
not take note of the extensive natural history sites and rare species which occur
within the project area; nor does it state that any of these will be "salvaged" prior
to the construction of the dam or the filling of the pool.  This is a serious omis­
sion.  Samples of the aquatic and terrestrial plants and animals which occupy Salt
Creek and its floodplain area should certainly be collected and carefully preserved in
established research museum collections before they and their habitat are irreversibly
and irretrievably destroyed by the construction of this dam.  These specimens,
properly documented, would be of inestimable value in evaluating the actual environ­
mental impact of the project, if the project is completed.  They will help biologists
of future generations to know something of the native fauna and flora of Ohio in an
area which will by then have been destroyed.

These specimens will also be extremely valuable in predicting the probable en­
vironmental impact of projects such as this one which may be proposed in the future.
It is essential that we be able to foresee at least the most important of the many
subtle and often intricate long-term effects of our changing the environment in
which we live before we make changes which may result in making this planet uninhab­
itable for future generations of mankind.  Only by carefully studying the actual ef­
fects of future engineering schemes.

Any evaluation of the environmental impact of the project depends upon the scale
of values assigned by the evaluators.  Assigning the U. S. Army Corps of Engineers to
evaluate the probable impact of the project which they are to build is not unlike
asking a beaver to evaluate the impact of a beaver dam, or a hungry child to object­
ively evaluate the benefit-to-cost ratio of an ice cream cone.  If the best interests
of £he whole population are to be served, the probable effects of the construction
of such a project must be studied in advance by competent but objective specialists
who represent all of the people who will be affected in the long run by the project.
They will be more likely to present an unbiased opinion if their jobs or contracts
do not depend on their ability to demonstrate that the benefits will exceed the costs
to the taxpayers and the environment.  Just as the best interests of the public are
served if concerned, objective biologists and health authorities set the standards of
ailuedble pollution, so the public will be best served if concerned, objective ecolo­
gists and sociologists are allowed to determine the extent to which our natural en­
vironment shall be destroyed.

Possible alternatives to the dam project should be seriously considered.  As
noted in the Environmental Statement, Vinton County, which contains the major portion
of the area to be acquired for the project, is one of the more depressed counties of
Ohio.  Yet much of the best farmland in Vinton County is in the portion of the Salt
Creek valley which will be flooded by the proposed dam.  It is difficult to see how

[PDF page 56]
^fcstro^ing this productive land will contribute to the livelihood and prosperity of
the;..  residents of Vinton County.  Are the loss of these productive farms and the
tax revenue they generate,  the loss of the biologically rich stream with, its scenic
qualities, its natural recreation potential, and its noted fishery,  truly less im-
portant in the long run than a few extfa jobs and additional acres of water surface
for recreation?  Is the potential flood protection the project would give the down­
stream communities truly of greater importance than the damage which would be caused
by permanently flooding the rich Vinton County farmland?

As the Environmental Statement notes, there are a number of possible alterna­
tive ways to achieve flood control and develop the recreation potential of Salt
Creek without building the proposed dam.  Most of these alternatives would provide
less revenue to the Corps of Engineers and their contracting firms, but they would
save the American taxpayer great sums of money, and some of them undoubtedly would
have better long-range environmental effects.

The zoning of low-lying areas to control further development on flood plains
certainly seems to be a very sensible and promising alternative to impoundment of the
stream.  If the floodplain land were zoned as open space for agricultural and recre­
ational uses, the highland sites couldbereserved for woodlands, homes, industries,
and other structures.  If this were done, then the rivers of our country could be
allowed to run free, with their valuable fisheries and their aesthetic values largely
unimpaired by unwise development and pollution.  The taxpayers would pay far less for
flood control projects, since they would not be needed.  Homeowners on the uplands
could enjoy the aesthetic values of open space and wild lands near their homes.  The
enormous economic damage and loss of life which now occur when a major river over­
flows its banks would be far less if flood plains were zoned for use only by such
structures and activities as would not be harmed by periodic flooding.

As the Environmental Statement notes, "Alternatives to the project that would
result in increased recreational use or in increased quality of use include the pro­
vision of public access areas and recreational facilities along parts of the stream,
implementation of a program of fishery management in the stream and wildlife manage­
ment in the area, and an increase in the recreational development in nearby State
and National forests."  Such alternatives, combined with proper floodplain zoning,
could very likely achieve all of the benefits of the proposed dam, as well as make
a far more stable and long-lasting step toward a high quality environment for all
mankind— and at far less cost to the taxpayer than the proposed dam.

Such alternatives should be given careful and objective consideration by a con­
cerned jury representative of the people.  They should recognize that a dam would be
a costly and strictly temporary solution to the problem of flooding, since, as even
the Corps of Engineers admits (page 8)

"The project was formulated on the basis of having an economic
life of 100 years.  The physical life of the project will likely
be considerably in excess of that period.  Major rehabilitation
or reallocation cf storages may be required upon expiration of
the project life."

However, a thoughtful program of flood-plain zoning and development of recreational
resources, carried out gradually at little expense over the next hundred years,
could provide the benefits of a beautiful and relatively unaltered natural environ­
ment, largely undamaged by periodic flooding, as a heritage for our great-great
grandchildren.  Will they not appreciate this far more than a weedy mudflat behind an
ancient wall, with crowded industrial cities huddled behind other walls along the
rivers far downstream?  The choice is ours.

12 February 1971
